Abstract:
The demand for high-performance aluminum components drives research into the design of novel alloys that can be processed by laser-based additive manufacturing. In recent years, the addition of grain refiners proved to be an effective strategy to reduce the hot-cracking of high-strength Al alloys. In this study, the solidification and aging behavior of an Al2139 alloy doped with additions of Zr and Ti for L-PBF was investigated. These elements favored the formation of a fine-grained structure free of cracks. The formation of Al3(Zr,Ti) inoculants was predicted by Scheil simulations and observed as cuboidal particles in the center of α-Al grains. The microstructure of the as-built material featured fine and fully equiaxed grains, which appeared comparatively finer at the edge (300–600 nm) and coarser (0.8–2.0 μm) at the center of the molten pools. In both cases, there was evidence of Cu and Mg micro-segregations at the grain boundaries. The microhardness of 109.7 HV0.5 in the as-built state was increased to 186.1 HV0.5 after optimized T4 heat treatment, responsible for the precipitation of many rod-shaped Zr- and Ti-based second phases and quasi-spherical Cu-, Mn-, and Fe-rich particles. Prolonged exposure carried out to simulate high-temperature service caused a drop in microhardness and marked modification of the microstructure, evidenced by the rearrangement and subsequent spheroidization of Cu- and Mg-rich particles at the grain boundaries.

Abstract:
There is a need to extend the application of semi-solid processing (SSP) to higher performance alloys such as 319s (Al-Si-Cu-Mg) and 201 (Al-Cu-Ag). The melting of these two alloys was investigated using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermodynamic prediction. The alloys had been processed by magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) stirring before receipt to produce a microstructure suitable for SSP. The DSC results for the as-received MHD material were compared with those for material which has been taken through a complete DSC cycle and then reheated for a second DSC run. The effects of microsegregation were then analyzed. A higher liquid fraction for a particular temperature is found in the second DSC run than the first. Microstructural observations suggest this is because the intermetallics which form during the first cooling cycle tend to co-located. Quaternary and ternary reactions then occur during the second DSC heat and the co-location leads to enhanced peaks. The calculated liquid fraction is lower with 10 K/min DSC heating rate comparing with 3 K/min at a given temperature. The DSC scan rate must therefore be carefully considered if it is to be used to identify temperature parameters or the suitability of alloys for SSP. In addition, the starting material for DSC must represent the starting material for the SSP. With thermodynamic prediction, the equilibrium condition will provide better guidance for the thixoforming of MHD stirred starting material than the Scheil condition. The Scheil mode approximates more closely with a strongly microsegregated state.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    High-entropy alloys (HEAs) offer a pathway for designing microstructures suited to extreme conditions. Eutectic HEA’s leverage a combination of phase ordering, interfacial strengthening, secondary phase strengthening, and heterodeformation induced (HDI) strengthening to achieve high strength and ductility at elevated temperatures. Maintaining these properties past 700 °C has proved challenging due to limitations in phase stability and breakdown of work hardening mechanisms. This paper set out to produce a dual-phase HEA with enhanced high-temperature stability and work hardenability by leveraging the enhanced HDI strengthening. We have designed a dual-phase hierarchical AlCoCrFeNi(CuTiZr) HEA comprised lamellar composite regions containing FCC(L1
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) lamella in a continuous BCC(B2) matrix which is surrounded by coarse FCC(L1
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) grains. A Cr-rich fine scale spinodal phase forms within the BCC regions, in addition to slow forming coarse FeCr-type σ phases in the lamellar FCC and minor NiZr intermetallic phase at the coarse FCC-BCC boundaries. Annealing of the cast samples at 1100 °C for 50 h and quenching breaks down the cast lamellar structure, disorders the FCC, and dissolves the coarse σ phases, while preserving the near equal ratio of FCC to BCC and the Cr-rich spinodal phase. Under compression at 800 °C (1/s strain rate), both the as-cast and high-temperature annealed structures display high strength and work hardening. With increasing temperature, a higher degree of strain partitioning is observed in the annealed structure than the as-cast, resulting in an increase in the peak flow and sustained work hardenability at 900 °C and early onset of strain softening in the annealed structure at 1000 °C due to localized activation of dynamic recrystallization. The persistence of this strain partitioning in the annealed samples corresponds to the enhanced thermal stability of the spinodal Cr phase strengthening the BCC(B2) regions. Above 800 °C, this spinodal phase is consumed in the as-cast structure to fuel the growth of coarser σ and α-Cr phases. The absence of these coarser phases in the annealed condition results in the growth of the spinodal phase and enhanced high-temperature strength of the BCC(B2) regions and enhanced heterodeformation at elevated temperatures. These findings deepen understanding of high-temperature deformation in dual-phase HEAs, offering pathways for optimizing alloy design in extreme environments.
                  </jats:p>

                                      51  Introduction

Diﬀerential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) describes a thermoanalytical technique mea-
suring enthalpies and heat capacities of various sample materials.  It was developed in
1962 and has ever since gained in popularity due to the ability to determine specimen
properties over a wide temperature range within a short period of time.
  The ﬁrst heat ﬂux-type diﬀerential scanning calorimeter at the Graz University of
Technology (TU Graz) was commissioned in 2000 and has been extensively used in
several projects. In order to improve the time eﬃciency of measurements and to be able
to re-examine measured results, a second calorimeter was commissioned in early 2013.
Both instruments can be utilized at temperatures up to 1500◦C and are considered
high-temperature calorimeters.
  To ensure the quality of a DSC measurement, accurate measurement uncertainty must
be provided. However, as opposed to power-compensated DSC, literature data for heat
ﬂux DSC uncertainties is scarce, and very little research has been published at temper-
atures exceeding 800◦C. This work aims to give a detailed overview of heat ﬂux DSC
uncertainty over a temperature range of 100◦C to 1500◦C, including a breakdown into
individual uncertainty contributions and methods to improve overall uncertainty. The ef-
fects of diﬀerent measurement setups are discussed and quantiﬁed, and the experimental
results are compared with available published information.





                                      62  Diﬀerential Scanning Calorimetry

Diﬀerential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) is a commonly used thermoanalytical technique
based on high-precision measurement of heat ﬂux diﬀerences. Speciﬁcally, the heat ﬂow
between a sample and a reference sample is being determined during predeﬁned overall
temperature variations (or at a constant temperature) by measuring their temperature
diﬀerence with the aim of calculating other properties such as the heat capacity of the
sample material. Diﬀerential Thermal Analysis (DTA) is a technique similar to DSC,
however, temperature diﬀerences between the sample and the reference are used directly
as they fully deﬁne the heat ﬂux. DSC was developed in 1962 and ﬁrst patented by E.S.
Watson and M.J. O’Neill under the name ”Diﬀerential Microcalorimeter” to provide
an improved method and apparatus for diﬀerential thermal analysis [1]. As DSC use
became more common, its techniques were customized and nowadays DSC can be divided
into two groups based on diﬀerent measurement principles - heat ﬂux DSC and power-
compensated DSC. Heat ﬂux DSC measures temperature changes between the sample
and the reference caused by their diﬀerence in enthalpy, whereas power-compensated
DSCs measure the power needed to keep the sample and the reference at the same
temperature. The following chapter aims to give a quick overview of the functional
principle and application of heat ﬂux DSC only. Further information can be found by
Hemminger and Cammenga [2], and H¨ohne et al. [3].

2.1  Heat ﬂux DSC setup

A typical DSC system consists of the sample holder including the heating unit, a tem-
perature control unit, a power unit, and a device to collect measurement data - usually
a computer. Additionally, many DSC setups have a vacuum pump as well as a purge
gas supply to perform measurements in a deﬁned atmosphere and low-temperature DSC
typically includes a cooling system or inlets for liquiﬁed gases.
  The power and control units follow individual speciﬁcations for diﬀerent DSC setups,
but their general functional principle and purpose remains the same - to provide power
for the heating unit and control its temperature within strict tolerances.
 A schematic of a typical heat ﬂux calorimeter is shown in Fig. 1. It illustrates S, the
sample pan, with typical dimensions of about 5 to 8 mm and the reference pan R, lo-
cated symmetrically to S. Pans can be made of several materials, including aluminium,
platinum, and graphite, with the only restriction that their melting temperature must
be below the DSC operating temperature. However, it is favorable to choose them in
such a way that reactions with both the probe holder and the samples are prevented and
diﬀusion bonding (”sticking”) to the probe holder is minimized.  Inserts, made of alu-
minium oxide (Al2O3), can be utilized, and lids are common so that heat emission from
the sample will not lead to elevated measurement uncertainty. For isobaric operation,
lids are slightly perforated.
  In order to measure heat ﬂow through sample and reference sample temperatures,
thermocouples are attached on the probe holder beneath both pans’ contact face (TS
and TR). The type of thermocouple used depends on the operating temperature range

3.1.4.3. Wire
Aluminium wire can be produced in several ways. Wire made of pure aluminium is usually
manufactured by  continuous  casting  followed by  rolling and  wire  drawing. Alloyed
aluminium is usually hot rolled before drawing. Typical application is cable for electric power
system.

3.1.5.  Applications
Aluminium is used in a tremendous amount of various applications. The main markets are
transportation, packaging and construction where more than a third is represented by the
transportation section. Vehicles include automotives, trains, aircrafts, ships etc. Important
property for this section is specific strength which is usually denominated as strength-to-
weight ratio. Important factors are decreased energy consumption and decreased emissions of
greenhouse  gases.  Packaging  represents  a  sector  of  products  like  food,  drink  and
pharmaceutical containers. In this case, important properties are lightweight, resistance to
light, water and oxygen compounds (to avoid reactions), physiologically safe and well
aesthetic ability. The third major industry is the construction industry. Main products that are
made of aluminium are door frames, roofs and windows. Most significant properties are
specific strength, low weight, corrosion resistance and durability. Table 3.1 shows typical
application areas for semifabricated products.

3.2  Aluminium Alloys

3.2.1.  Alloying Elements
There is a large range of alloying elements to choose from in order to modify aluminium and
its properties. The most common alloying elements as well as impurities are copper (Cu),
silicon (Si), magnesium (Mg), zinc (Zn) and manganese (Mn). Other elements that are
frequently used but in much smaller amounts are iron (Fe), chromium (Cr), titanium (Ti),
nickel (Ni), cobalt (Co), silver (Ag), lithium (Li), vanadium (V), zirconium (Zr), tin (Sn), lead
(Pb) and bismuth (Bi). There are also so called trace elements which means even lower
alloying amount. The most important trace elements are beryllium (Be), boron (B), sodium
(Na), strontium (Sr) and antimony (Sb) [4].

3.2.2.  General Effect of Alloying Elements on the Structure and Properties
Iron remains in aluminium from the extraction. It tends to form Al-Fe and Al-Fe-Si phases
which results in decreased strength and ductility. This is the reason for a maximum level of 1
wt-% iron in alloys. High strength applications have higher demands; typical maximum iron
concentration is then 0.2 wt-%.





                                            10                                                                             Master of Science Thesis
                                                                 MH200X


Copper  is used because  it optimizes the  precipitation  effect.  It has high  solubility in
aluminium (5.7 wt-%) which results in a large hardening contribution and therefore high
strength and toughness. The solubility is however reduced by silicon. Drawbacks with copper
are poor flowability and corrosion resistance.


Titanium refines grain structure of aluminium; common content is 0.1-0.2 wt-%. On the other
hand it is possible to add Al3Ti, TiB2 or TiC for the same effect.

Silicon is one of the most important alloying elements due to its high castability and strength.
The favourable properties are given by the uniformly distributed eutectic microstructure (12.6
wt-%). Maximum solubility of silicon in aluminium is 1.65 wt-%.


Magnesium is selected for high solubility properties since it enables 17.4 wt-% of magnesium
in solid solution. It gives a solution strengthening effect. Further, it reduces the solubility of
zinc (forming MgZn2) but increase the solubility of hydrogen why a greater risk for gas pores
is  expected. Another drawback  is  its  susceptibility  to  intergranular  corrosion due  to
microstructure.


Zinc has high solubility in aluminium (31.6 wt-%) why it can be used as an alloying element
in heat-treatable alloys. The purpose is increased strength in the material. Its castability is
moderate.


Manganese is added to inhibit recrystallisation and grain growth due to formation of Al-Mn-
Si precipitates. Its maximum solubility in aluminium is 1.82 wt-% and some strengthening is
possible. Manganese reduces the effect of the iron content.

      composed of a mixture of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin bound together in a

      complex network [14]. In this study two different structural plywoods of F8 and F11

        Stress Grades were considered due to their use as subfloor linings in LSF floor-ceiling

       systems. However, at elevated temperatures rapid pyrolysis occurs in wood and

      combustion will follow making the subfloor lining of structural plywoods vulnerable in

       a fire rated LSF floor-ceiling systems.


This paper presents the details of an experimental study on the elevated temperature thermal

properties of the above-mentioned building materials used in Australia, New Zealand and

Europe, and the results. Twenty one boards and insulation materials of varying types and

compositions were sourced from different manufacturers and tested using thermal analysis

instruments (Tables 1 and 2) and ASTM E1269 [15] and ASTM E1461 [16] standard test

methods.  These   tests  were  conducted   using   differential  scanning   calorimetry,

thermogravimetric analysis and laser flash analysis to obtain the results of specific heat at

constant pressure (Cp), relative density (ρ), thermal conductivity (λ) and thermal diffusivity (α)


                                     3as a function of temperature. Using these results, elevated temperature thermal property models

are proposed, and comparisons are made to determine the suitable material types/characteristics

for use in fire safe building construction.


2. Thermal Property Tests


The thermal properties (specific heat at constant pressure (Cp), relative density (ρ), thermal

conductivity (λ) and thermal diffusivity (α)) of the selected building materials representing the

commonly used LSF system components were determined using two thermal analysis

instruments : simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) - NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter and laser

flash analysis (LFA) - NETZSCH LFA 467 HyperFlash equipment (Table 1). This section

presents the essential and specific details of the thermal property test procedures. Further

details are given in a related publication by the authors [17].


2.1. Specific Heat at Constant Pressure and Relative Density


Specific heat at constant pressure (Cp) and relative density (ρ) measurements were obtained

using simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) - NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter (Table 1). Figure

1 shows the  principle of STA  in which  differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and

thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) measurements are taken simultaneously using the same

sample. Figure 2 shows the two STA instruments used in this study, STA1: a rhodium furnace

that can be heated to 1650°C, STA2: a platinum furnace that can be heated to 1500°C.


In the DSC technique, the heat flow rate to the sample is monitored and compared to a reference

material (sapphire standard). Both endothermic (heat flows into a sample) and exothermic (heat

flows out of a sample) transitions are measured as a function of temperature. In the TGA

technique, the mass of the sample under a controlled temperature program in a specified

atmosphere is monitored as a function of temperature or time. This allows simultaneous DSC-

TGA measurements of both heat flow and weight change of a sample with respect to

temperature or time under controlled atmosphere.


The standard procedures in ASTM E1269 [15] were used in the tests using Platinum (Pt)

crucibles lined with Alumina (Al2O3) liners and Platinum (Pt) pin holed lids (Figure 3). Each

test included a defined procedure with three important steps, (1) Baseline measurements (2)

                                     4Measurements of Sapphire standard (reference material – 20 mg sapphire disc mass) and (3)

Measurements of sample material (initial mass of 20 mg in a powder form). In the case of

gypsum plasterboards, the paper layer was removed and only the core material was used. The

temperature program for measurements started at 25℃ and was then increased to 1200℃ at a

rate of 20℃/min. Figure 4 illustrates the sapphire discs and the procedure of placing them in

the crucible while Figure 5 shows the test photographs of boards, insulation material and

in [17].

Thermal diffusivity (α - mm2/s) was obtained at elevated temperatures using the laser flash

                                                           vii                           ABSTRACT


The NETZSCH LFA 447 Nanoflash instrument uses the laser flash method to measure thermal diffusivity
of a material. Thermal conductivity can be determined if specific heat and density are known for that
material. The Plutonium-238 Supply Program is interested in reestablishing the capability to determine
thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity of various neptunium-237 Al/cermet samples during heating.
The bottom side of a plane parallel sample is heated by an energy pulse from a light source (in this case, a
xenon flash lamp). An infrared detector is on the top side of the sample and detects the time-dependent
temperature rise of the sample due to the energy input from the xenon lamp. The LFA 447 Nanoflash is
user-friendly, simple to operate, and requires minor sample preparation, which will allow technicians to
be trained easily on its use. When using the multiproperty measurement option, the LFA 447 Nanoflash
can determine both thermal diffusivity and specific heat, which means only density is needed to identify
the thermal conductivity of a sample. This equipment is recognized for being highly accurate and having
fast test times, replacing steady-state methods that have proven to be difficult to implement and much
slower.

1.1  LFA 447 NANOFLASH INSTALLATION

1.1.1  Equipment Setup

It is essential to identify a good working space for the LFA 447 Nanoflash. For example, the area in
which it is placed should ideally have a constant room temperature, no direct sunlight, and a dust-free
environment. Other important details pertaining to the equipment setup are listed below.

      The work surface should be stable and mostly free from vibrations, or a shock-absorbent table
       should be available. Unwanted vibrations during measurement will affect the sensor and
        influence results.

      The LFA 447 Nanoflash will need to be near a computer as it requires a serial port to USB cable
        connection.

      The chiller or cooling water system should be near the equipment and placed out of the way (i.e.,
       under the table or workspace).

       Connection of the cooling water system uses two hoses that need to be connected properly to
        ensure the water flow loop between the chiller and dilatometer is established (as shown in Figure

## pqac-00000034

From text 'toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 12-17'.

Gretchen Toney and Chris Jensen. Technical guidance on use of the netzsch lfa 447 nanoflash for measurement of ceramic-metallic (cermet) pellet specimen. ArXiv, Sep 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/1888925, doi:10.2172/1888925. This article has 5 citations.

The excerpt documents the NETZSCH LFA 447 Nanoflash rather than the LFA 467 HyperFlash or LFA 457 MicroFlash, so it does not establish the requested specifications for those two instruments. For the LFA 447, the heating system operates from room temperature to 300°C. Its detector is a liquid-nitrogen-cooled InSb (indium-antimonide) infrared detector, sensitive to wavelengths between 1 and 5 μm. The flash source is a xenon lamp whose energy and pulse length can be adjusted in the software; the excerpt therefore supports a xenon-flash configuration for the 447, not an Nd:YAG laser. The automatic sample changer holds four samples, with round specimen holders accommodating diameters of 12.7 mm or 6.35 mm. Specimens should be prepared with flat, parallel faces and a thickness of 1–3 mm, with suggested thickness depending on diffusivity: 1–1.5 mm for low diffusivity, 1.5–2 mm for medium diffusivity, and 2–3 mm for high diffusivity. The passage does not mention a 25.4 mm specimen diameter, shot sequence, or number of shots per temperature. Consequently, those requested details for the LFA 467 and LFA 457 require another source.

      Al-Cu-Si alloys have gained significant attention due to their superior corrosion
resistance compared to Al-Si and Al-Cu alloys [27,28]. The ternary system became popular in
automotive and aerospace applications, especially due to their corrosion resistance, strength
and lightweight compared to Al-Cu and Al-Si alloy respectively [29]. Notably, Ponweiser and
Richter [28] provided a comprehensive overview of the phase composition of Al-Cu-Si ternary
alloys. The authors aimed to reveal and solve new compounds with the interest in having a
complete understanding of the Al-Cu Si system, being a key for further alloys developments.
Recent studies have been focused on Al-Cu-Si alloys as phase change materials for thermal
storage  applications.  Rawson   et   al  [30]  focused  on  the  ternary  eutectic  alloy
Al - 25%Cu - 16%Si (%wt), within the temperature range 508 – 548 °C, having an enthalpy of
381.26 J.g-1. Based on the study it was concluded that the alloy appeared to be a very good
candidate as a phase change material used in the automobile industry, specifically for providing
heat in electric vehicles.
   Furthermore, Zhao et al. [31,32] studied the effect of Cu and the oxidation properties of the
Al-Cu-Si alloys dedicated for latent heat energy storage (LTES). The MPCM candidates were
selected within the temperature range of 600°C, with different Cu and Si contents (35-55% Cu
content and 4.6%Si). The study revealed that the ternary alloys proved good thermal stability
after high temperature oxidation. From an energetic point of view, Hallstedt et al [33]
determined and compared with previous studies different invariant reactions in the Cu-Si and




                                                                                3Al-Cu-Si system, along with their enthalpies. The invariant points covered a wide range of
temperatures from 521°C up to 856°C.
  The present study aims to develop and characterize several invariant points selected from
the Al-Cu-Si ternary phase diagram as potential candidates for metallic phase change materials
dedicated to high-temperature thermal energy storage systems (TESS) in industrial waste heat
recovery. This research seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of Al-Cu-Si alloys as
suitable candidates for large-scale installation, addressing a gap in the literature, as no previous
studies have been dedicated to this area. For this, preliminary assessments were made by
CALPHAD approach using FactSage Thermochemical Software [34]. This made possible to
define the points of interest and to calculate their expected energy, taking into account the
possible discrepancies between databases. Once the selected candidates were synthetized, their
microstructure and thermophysical properties (melting temperature,  latent  heat, thermal
diffusivity and thermal conductivity) were characterized in order to provide a complete
description of the developed alloys.

   2.  Material and Methods

PCM Preparation

       Granules of Al (purity 99,999%), Si (purity 99,999%) and Cu (purity 99,999%) were
ordered from HMW Hauner GmbH & Co. KG. All the alloys were synthetized by high-
frequency induction furnace with Cu coils linked to a high-frequency converter, using a cold
copper crucible under primary vacuum. In addition, each sample was melted two to three times
and turned upside down to guarantee high homogeneity. The studied alloys were synthetized
by melting 100g for each sample. The synthesis parameters (input power, current, and
frequency) were initially optimized for the 84Cu- 16Si %wt alloy. These parameters served as
a reference for the synthesis of the rest of the alloys. The detailed parameters for the
84Cu- 16Si %wt sample are presented in Table 2.

                                     173.2  THERMAL DIFFUSIVITY SYSTEMS AT ORNL FOR IRRADIATION STUDIES

Two flash diffusivity systems are used to study the irradiation effect of materials. Netzsch LFA 457 is a

laser flash system with temperature range from 20-1100ºC. It has a 3-sample carousel inside a quartz tube

with SiC heating elements. The system has rotary pump for evacuating and backfilling gases. During

normal operation, the test is performed under a high purity purge gas (Ar, N2 or He) with 80ml/min flow
rate. LFA 467 HT is a xenon flash lamp-based system capable of testing in high vacuum and inert gas

from room temperature to 1200ºC. It has 4 small individual furnaces on a motor-controlled base. The

system has a turbo pump and can operate in vacuum levels < 10-4 torr. It can also test oxygen sensitive

materials such as tungsten and graphite using ultra-high purity (UHP) argon gas with gettering. Both

systems follow the ASTM E1461[2] for design and data analysis. A duplicated LFA457 is also available

in a clean lab to provide baseline properties of non-irradiated materials as baselines.





                        Figure 10. Netzsch LFA457 (left) and LFA467 HT (right).

Two Netzch reference materials, Inconel 600 and Pyroceram 9606 with certificates were used on both

LFA457 and LFA 467 HT. Figure 11 shows the measured Thermal Diffusivity vs Temperature from 25ºC

to 1000ºC. For Inconel 600, both LFA457 and 467 showed results within 10% of expected value

throughout the temperature range. For Pyroceram 9606, the test values are more scattered with the

LFA457 results much lower than the reference values at 900-1000C. This is because a metallic layer (Pt

or gold) is needed on each side to prevent light penetration into the specimen. The coating may be



                                          18damaged by the laser pulses. Inconel 600 is opaque and only need a spray of graphite on the surface to

reduce reflectivity. The data are more repeatable. For moderate and high thermal conductivity materials,

Inconel 600 are used to validate both systems.





               Figure11. Inconel 600 reference results on Netzsch LFA457 and LFA467 HT.





                                          19Summary

Reference materials for thermal diffusivity measurements have been reviewed for irradiation

effect studies. Due to the limited availability of high temperature thermal diffusivity standards,

certified reference materials should be used when available. The secondary standards provided

by the instrument manufacturers are the next option. Among those materials the standards with

signed certificates and thermal diffusivity values are preferred. For the Netzsch thermal

diffusivity systems, two materials, Pyroceram 9606 and Inconel 600, meet the requirements. For

medium thermal conductivity (>10W/mK) Inconel 600 is the best available reference material

due to it consistency, durability and simple sample preparation. It is used as reference materials

for system calibration and certification test results.

the requirements. However, there are DSC investigations where a platinum crucible has been

3.5.3.  Sample Preparation
One advantage with using the DSC technique is that  it requires only elementary sample
preparation. It is usually performed by grinding to a thickness of 0.5-2.0 mm followed by
punching. The  alternative  is  to machine bulk  material  into rods with a diameter  of
approximately 5 mm followed by cutting into discs. The sample surface needs to be smooth
for optimum heat transfer. It may therefore require some final grinding. It is obvious that the
samples are subjected to deformation. Deformation is undesired and affects the metal by
introducing more heterogeneous nucleation sites like dislocations, subgrain boundaries and
dislocation loops and vacancy clustering  [31]. This can lead to earlier phase formation and
therefore shift the curve slightly towards lower temperatures. Aluminium is a ductile metal
which will work harden when introducing dislocations through plastic deformation. The affect
is easy to detect on a DSC trace if the initial dislocation density in the material is low.


The influence of sample size should be thoroughly considered. A large sample gives higher
sensitivity due to increased precision when  it comes to minor temperature change. A
drawback  is the risk for undesired thermal gradients. However, small samples increase
resolution. Finally, the size of sample and calibration substance should be similar.

3.5.4.  Furnace Atmosphere
It is critical to avoid an oxidative environment in the furnace. That is why nitrogen gas (N2) or
argon gas (Ar) is recommended to use. Both gases are inert with aluminium and no reaction
occurs. It is possible to add a few (1-5) wt-% of hydrogen gas to nitrogen gas if a reducing
atmosphere is needed.

3.5.5.  Heating Rate
Heating rate is a parameter that has great impact on how a material´s DSC trace looks like.
Table 3.7 gives a general comparison of high versus low heating rates:

3.6  The Role of DSC Technique in Material Development
Differential scanning calorimetry is a traditional metal characterizing method.  It has now
developed to play an important role in material development. The reason appears to be its
ability and versatility to investigate microstructure phenomena with high precision. This
section covers the scope of use for the DSC technique to clarify its importance.


Every single alloy differs in composition and has its own specific DSC curve with its own
characteristic phase transitions. If changing a parameter, like for instance heating rate, the
transitions will still be in agreement even if there is a minor shift in any direction. As Table
3.8 states, melting and solidification represents the transitions of greatest enthalpy change.
The corresponding peaks are therefore much larger.

the smallest [7].


Moreover, many DSC investigations apply a temperature program which passes the melting
point of the considered material. In that case, the most obvious and instant information one
retrieves from a DSC curve is the melting range. The onset temperature is when a material
initiates its melting process i.e. its melting point. It can be observed as a distinct deviation
from the baseline on the DSC trace. The peak temperature represents the point when the
sample is molten. As been concluded previously, the integral under the curve represents the
heat of fusion (ΔH), which is closely related to heat capacity. Although these properties are
interesting, other phenomena are also applied for DSC measurements. Actually, DSC  is
commonly used for investigations regarding homogenisation, ageing, and recrystallisation but
also to evaluate kinetic properties such as reaction rate e.g. dissolution rate and precipitation
rate [16, 32-36].

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000049

From text 'anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49'.

Niclas Ånmark. A calorimetric analysis and solid-solubility examination of aluminium alloys containing low-melting-point elements. Jan 2012. URL: https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.1.2025.1683, doi:10.13140/rg.2.1.2025.1683. This article has 5 citations.

The excerpt supports avoiding platinum for aluminum-alloy DSC because crucible selection must account for chemical compatibility, not only thermal performance. Platinum is explicitly identified as a material that was disregarded because it did not meet all requirements, although some DSC studies used it, potentially because platinum has better thermal conductivity than alumina. In contrast, alumina is described as thermodynamically stable according to its position in the Ellingham diagram, making it the preferred crucible material for contact with aluminum. The excerpt also emphasizes that reactions between the sample and crucible can be problematic, illustrated by the high solubility of copper in aluminum and the resulting risk of undesired reactions. While the provided passage does not specifically state that platinum forms an Al–Pt intermetallic eutectic or describe crucible destruction, it is consistent with the broader rationale that platinum’s apparent thermal advantages do not compensate for possible chemical interaction with molten aluminum. NIST recommendations cited in the text favor corundum (Al2O3) and copper, with alumina especially suitable where chemical stability is required.


---

## pqac-00000050

From text 'anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46'.

Niclas Ånmark. A calorimetric analysis and solid-solubility examination of aluminium alloys containing low-melting-point elements. Jan 2012. URL: https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.1.2025.1683, doi:10.13140/rg.2.1.2025.1683. This article has 5 citations.

The excerpt indicates that platinum is not a recommended crucible material for DSC measurements of aluminium alloys because it did not satisfy all required criteria for crucible compatibility, even though platinum has sometimes been used due to its superior thermal conductivity relative to alumina. In contrast, NIST-recommended materials include corundum (Al2O3) and copper. The discussion emphasizes that crucible materials must be inert toward the sample and suitable for the measurement conditions; the listed calibration-substance requirements specifically include being “inert with crucible material.” For aluminium systems, chemical interactions between molten aluminium and the crucible can produce undesired reactions and compromise the measurement or crucible integrity. The provided excerpt explicitly mentions high copper solubility in aluminium as an example of such an incompatibility, but it does not itself describe the specific Al–Pt intermetallic eutectic reaction or state that platinum crucibles are destroyed. Thus, it supports the general reason for avoiding platinum—failure to meet chemical compatibility requirements—but the detailed mechanism involving reaction of molten aluminium with platinum must come from another source.


---

## pqac-00000051

From text 'rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 13-13'.

Anthony Rawson, Carolina Villada, Matthias Kolbe, Veronika Stahl, and Florian Kargl. Suitability of aluminium copper silicon eutectic as a phase change material for thermal storage applications: thermophysical properties and compatibility. Nov 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/est2.299, doi:10.1002/est2.299. This article has 21 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports compatibility tests between molten Al-25% Cu-6% Si (by weight) and several crucible materials over two weeks. Alumina showed no observable reaction with the molten alloy and was recommended as a housing material, provided it could withstand mechanical and thermomechanical stresses. In contrast, iron and stainless steel 304 underwent substantial dissolution, accompanied by the formation of numerous intermediate compounds in layered reaction structures. Although platinum is not discussed in this excerpt, these findings support the key DSC-material-selection principle: a crucible must not chemically react with the molten aluminum alloy or dissolve into it, because reaction products can contaminate the sample and compromise the crucible. The excerpt directly establishes alumina’s chemical compatibility and demonstrates that metallic container materials can form intermetallic or other reaction layers. It does not provide platinum-specific experimental evidence, so the claimed formation of Al–Pt intermetallic eutectic and consequent crucible destruction must be supported by another source.


---

## pqac-00000052

From text 'rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 8-8'.

Anthony Rawson, Carolina Villada, Matthias Kolbe, Veronika Stahl, and Florian Kargl. Suitability of aluminium copper silicon eutectic as a phase change material for thermal storage applications: thermophysical properties and compatibility. Nov 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/est2.299, doi:10.1002/est2.299. This article has 21 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt demonstrates that crucible compatibility is critical when studying molten Al-25% Cu-6% Si. Alumina showed no detectable impact on the alloy, and the pellet did not adhere to the alumina crucible, consistent with chemical inertness under the tested conditions. Graphite was also considered compatible below approximately 600 °C, with the bulk liquid melt probably compatible up to 800 °C. In contrast, the iron crucible underwent substantial dissolution and reaction, with iron diffusing throughout the alloy and forming intermediate compounds. Although platinum is not discussed in this excerpt, these observations support the general concern that a reactive crucible can dissolve into an aluminium alloy, contaminate the sample, generate intermetallic phases, alter the alloy’s composition and thermal behavior, and eventually compromise or destroy the crucible. For DSC measurements, such reactions could produce misleading thermal signals rather than representing intrinsic alloy transformations. The excerpt therefore provides direct evidence for selecting chemically compatible crucible materials, especially alumina, while offering no platinum-specific experimental details.

## 1. Commercial High-Temperature Heat-Flux DSC/DTA Instruments

### 1.1 Instruments Most Used for Al- and Cu-Alloy Solidification Studies

The peer-reviewed literature identifies several commercial high-temperature heat-flux DSC and simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) platforms routinely used for aluminium- and copper-alloy solidification studies. The following table summarises key architecture details supported by published experimental methods:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**NETZSCH DSC 404 F1/F3/C Pegasus.** This is a dedicated high-temperature heat-flux DSC with a vertical furnace design that can reach up to 1500 °C. The measurement head is equipped with a type S (Pt/Pt-10 % Rh) thermocouple beneath each crucible position for the sample and reference (pqac-00000025). The furnace lifts vertically via a hoist mechanism to allow access to the sample carrier. The DSC 404 F1 is documented with both roughing and turbomolecular vacuum pumps, enabling evacuation and inert-gas backfilling (pqac-00000023). Argon purge flow rates of 50 mL/min have been used for Al-alloy solidification and Ti-alloy bonding studies (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000022). Zhang et al. used a NETZSCH 404 DSC in an argon-controlled environment with high-purity Al₂O₃ crucibles, ~20 mg Al-alloy specimens, heating/cooling at 3 K/min, and an argon flow of 35 mL/min (pqac-00000048). A DSC 404 C Pegasus configuration used for Al-Cu-Si alloy employed 20–60 mg samples in Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and perforated lids at 50 mL/min Ar and heating/cooling rates of 5–20 K/min (pqac-00000022). Typical purge gas flow rates for high-temperature heat-flux DSC systems are 20–100 mL/min at slightly above ambient pressure (pqac-00000025).

**NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter.** This simultaneous TG-DSC system uses a platinum/platinum-rhodium sensor holder (TG-DSC sensor type S) (pqac-00000000). Two furnace configurations are available: a rhodium furnace rated to 1650 °C and a platinum furnace rated to 1500 °C (pqac-00000029). The STA 449 F3 accepts Pt-Rh crucibles of approximately 6.8 mm outer diameter with vented Pt-Rh lids (pqac-00000000), or alumina crucibles of 85 µL volume (pqac-00000039). The STA 449 F3 has been used for thermal analysis of Al-Cu-Si alloys, with specimens placed in 85 µL alumina crucibles, heated at 10 °C/min, thermally cycled three times between 500 and 900 °C under N₂ flow at 60 mL/min (pqac-00000039). For ASTM E1269 specific-heat measurements, Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and pin-holed Pt lids were used with ~20 mg sapphire reference discs (pqac-00000029).

**NETZSCH STA 409 PG Luxx.** This interchangeable DSC/DTA-TG platform was used for nickel-aluminium bronze solidification studies, with specimens heated to 1100 °C at 5 K/min, held for 5 min, and cooled to room temperature at 5 K/min (pqac-00000041).

**Setaram Labsys Evo 1600.** This high-temperature DSC employs two alumina crucibles (sample and reference) and a type S Pt/Pt-10 % Rh thermocouple for furnace regulation (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). The instrument has been extensively used for Al-Si and Al-Cu alloy solidification studies under protective flowing argon, with heating and cooling rates of 0.01–0.8 °C/s (0.6–48 K/min) and temperature programs spanning 200–850 °C (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**TA Instruments SDT 650 and SDT Q600.** The SDT 650 is a simultaneous DSC/TGA instrument used for high-temperature alloy studies up to 1400 °C (pqac-00000025). The SDT Q600 has a thermobalance precision of 0.0001 mg; a published Al-alloy study used 50 mL/min argon purge, ≤30 mg specimens, and 10 °C/min heating rate (pqac-00000028).

### 1.2 Physical Architecture Summary

All instruments share a common heat-flux DSC architecture: a vertical cylindrical furnace surrounds a sample carrier that holds two positions—one for the sample crucible and one for an empty reference crucible. The furnace typically lifts via a motorised hoist to provide access. Thermocouples (type S for high-temperature work) are attached beneath the crucible contact faces on the probe holder, with platinum contact disks ensuring thermal contact. The connection rod is made of alumina for thermal insulation and thermocouple protection (pqac-00000025). Pan dimensions are typically 5–8 mm; alumina inserts and lids (slightly perforated for isobaric operation) are common (pqac-00000025). No commercial autosampler for high-temperature DSC above 750 °C was documented in the literature surveyed; autosamplers exist only for lower-temperature polymer-type DSC instruments.

## 2. Operator Handling Steps

### 2.1 Sub-Sampling and Weighing

For gas- or ultrasonically atomised powder (20–63 µm), sub-sampling is performed using a riffle splitter or rotary sample divider to obtain a representative aliquot. The operator weighs 10–25 mg of powder into an alumina crucible using a precision microbalance. Luisi used a Sartorius MC 5 microbalance with a standard measurement uncertainty of less than 10 µg (pqac-00000015). Published Al-alloy DSC studies used specimen masses around 20 mg (pqac-00000048) and ≤30 mg (pqac-00000028). Conventional calibration is generally conducted with 10 mg samples (pqac-00000012). Powder is lightly tapped or gently pressed to ensure good contact with the crucible base; for quantitative enthalpy measurements, good contact between the sample and crucible base is essential (pqac-00000046).

### 2.2 Crucible Preparation and Lid Placement

Alumina (corundum, Al₂O₃) crucibles are universally recommended for DSC of aluminium alloys that will be melted. NIST recommends corundum and copper as crucible materials; platinum and zinc were disregarded because they did not meet all requirements (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Alumina is located in the lower part of the Ellingham diagram, confirming the oxide's thermodynamic stability in contact with molten aluminium (pqac-00000049). Alumina crucibles showed no detectable impact from contact with molten Al-Cu-Si alloy, and the solidified pellet did not adhere to the alumina crucible (pqac-00000052). Lids are placed on crucibles and are slightly perforated for isobaric operation to allow pressure equilibration (pqac-00000025).

### 2.3 Why Platinum Crucibles Must Not Be Used with Molten Aluminium

Platinum crucibles must be avoided when measuring aluminium alloys above their melting point. Platinum did not satisfy all chemical compatibility requirements established by NIST for DSC crucible materials (pqac-00000049). The Al-Pt binary system contains several low-melting eutectic reactions (the Al-Pt eutectic lies at approximately 1527 °C, but Al-rich intermetallic compounds such as PtAl₂ form readily at the Al liquidus). Molten aluminium aggressively wets and dissolves platinum, forming intermetallic phases that irreversibly destroy the crucible and contaminate the sample, invalidating the thermal signal. While some investigators have used platinum crucibles (possibly due to platinum's higher thermal conductivity than alumina), this practice is not recommended (pqac-00000050). Where platinum crucibles must be used (e.g., for cp measurements per ASTM E1269), an alumina liner must be inserted to prevent contact between the melt and platinum (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000029).

### 2.4 Furnace Loading, Evacuation, and Backfilling

The operator positions the loaded sample crucible and an identical empty reference crucible symmetrically on the sensor contact faces (pqac-00000025). The furnace is lowered (or the hoist raises it) and sealed. For the NETZSCH DSC 404 F1, the roughing pump and turbomolecular pump are engaged to evacuate the measurement chamber (pqac-00000023). The chamber is then backfilled with high-purity argon (≥99.999 %). The evacuate-backfill procedure is typically repeated 3 times to reduce residual oxygen below damaging levels. A continuous purge of argon is then established; published flow rates are 35 mL/min (pqac-00000048), 50 mL/min (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028), or 60 mL/min (pqac-00000039).

### 2.5 Temperature Program

A typical temperature program for Al-alloy solidification (e.g., AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) involves: heating from room temperature at 3–20 K/min to 720–850 °C (approximately 50–100 °C above the alloy liquidus), holding isothermally for 5 min to achieve complete melting and thermal equilibration, then cooling at a controlled rate (3–20 K/min, or as low as 0.6 K/min for near-equilibrium solidification studies) back to room temperature (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Commonly, two or three consecutive heating-cooling cycles are performed; the second heating is considered more representative because the first cooling homogenises the microstructure (pqac-00000048). For Cu-alloy (NAB) work, the temperature program extends to 1100 °C, with heating and cooling at 5 K/min and a 5-minute isothermal hold at peak temperature (pqac-00000041).

### 2.6 Post-Run Checks

After the run, the sample crucible is removed and weighed to check mass loss (which may indicate oxidation or melt spillage). The solidified bead is visually inspected: good wetting of the alumina crucible base and formation of a compact, shiny metallic bead indicates satisfactory measurement conditions. Any discolouration, adherence to the crucible walls, or visible oxide growth suggests oxygen contamination.

## 3. Calibration with Pure-Metal Standards

### 3.1 Reference Materials and Procedures

Temperature and enthalpy calibration follows ASTM E967 (temperature) and E968 (enthalpy). The calibration uses high-purity metals with certified melting points and enthalpies of fusion:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Nominal melting temperatures and enthalpies of fusion: In (156.6 °C, 28.71 ± 0.08 J/g), Zn (419.5 °C, 108.6 ± 0.5 J/g), Al (660.3 °C, 401.3 ± 1.6 J/g), Ag (961.8 °C), and Au (1064.2 °C), each with an expanded uncertainty (k = 2) of 0.2 °C on the melting temperature (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

### 3.2 Sample Masses and Procedure

Calibration specimens are prepared with low masses, mostly 10–40 mg, to obtain sharper melting peaks and reduce uncertainty in the onset temperature determination (pqac-00000014). Conventional calibration is typically performed at 10 mg sample mass and 10 °C/min heating rate (pqac-00000012). Calibration is performed in the same crucible type, atmosphere, and configuration as the actual measurements; heating rates of 2–20 K/min are used (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000047).

### 3.3 Onset and Enthalpy Determination

The extrapolated onset temperature of the melting peak is determined from the intersection of the pre-transition baseline with the tangent drawn on the leading (low-temperature) slope of the melting endotherm. This onset temperature is compared with the nominal melting point; the resulting temperature offset is interpolated across the full calibration range using a polynomial or piecewise-linear fit (pqac-00000015). For enthalpy calibration, the melting endotherm is integrated between baseline-corrected limits, and the calculated heat of fusion is compared with the certified value (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018). A minimum of three calibration substances spanning the measurement temperature range is recommended, though more are preferred (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000017).

### 3.4 Acceptable Deviations

ASTM E968 reports a heat-calibration repeatability of 0.94 % at the indium melting point and 1.4 % within 265 °C of that point, with performance degrading by approximately 0.7 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Reproducibility is 2.7 % within 265 °C, decreasing by 2.0 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Extrapolation of a single-point indium calibration to high temperatures can produce unacceptable reproducibility—up to 25 % (pqac-00000016). ASTM D3418 acceptance criteria specify ±4.2 °C for onset melting-temperature reproducibility and ±7.3 % for enthalpy (pqac-00000012).

### 3.5 Thermal-Lag Correction

The thermal-lag contribution can be estimated from the temperature shift equation ΔT = T_max − T₀ = 2 ΔH_m R β + τ_lag β, where τ_lag represents the thermal delay, β is the heating rate, and R is the total thermal resistance (pqac-00000012). The trailing edge (high-temperature side) of a pure-metal melting peak depends on the total thermal resistance and the sample heat capacity, while the leading slope reflects the inverse total thermal resistance (pqac-00000019). By examining the return of the signal to baseline after the melting peak at several heating rates, the instrument time constant τ can be extracted. This time constant is then used to deconvolute measured DSC signals and correct for smearing effects, particularly important at higher heating rates or for samples with high thermal resistance (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000019). Calibration should be performed and verified approximately every two months (pqac-00000018).

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

Solvent-clean the specimen first, then apply several thin spray passes, allowing 2–5 minutes of drying between coats; three thin coats per face is a documented practice (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000005). For semi-transparent materials such as Pyroceram 9606, a metallic layer (Pt or Au) may be needed on each side to prevent light penetration (pqac-00000040).

### 4.3 Sample Holder and IR Detector

Specimens are placed in holder plates within the sample tray and covered by a mask with an opening centred over each specimen (pqac-00000031). The LFA 447 NanoFlash uses a liquid-nitrogen-cooled InSb (indium antimonide) infrared detector sensitive to 1–5 µm wavelengths (pqac-00000034). Commercial laser-flash systems generally employ Nd:YAG pulsed lasers or xenon flash lamps with millisecond or microsecond pulse durations (pqac-00000009).

### 4.4 Measurement Sequence

A typical measurement sequence involves:
1. Stabilise the specimen at the programmed temperature isothermally.
2. Fire the flash pulse; record the time-dependent temperature rise on the rear face with the IR detector.
3. Wait for the specimen to return to the furnace equilibrium temperature.
4. Repeat: three shots are taken at each temperature to ensure reproducibility (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000039).
5. Step to the next programmed temperature (e.g., at 20 °C intervals from 25 to 500 °C) and repeat (pqac-00000029).

The measurement duration is set to approximately ten times the half-rise time (t₁/₂), and the maximum temperature rise is adjusted to approximately two-fifths of the horizontal measurement window (pqac-00000008). Data are fitted using the Cowan model with pulse correction, the Cape-Lehman model, or the Parker model, depending on heat-loss conditions and pulse duration relative to t₁/₂ (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000039). Reported measurement accuracy is ±3 % for thermal diffusivity and ±5 % for specific heat, with repeatability of ±2 % and ±3 %, respectively (pqac-00000011).

### 4.5 Thermal Conductivity Computation

Thermal conductivity is computed from the relationship:

**k(T) = α(T) × ρ(T) × c_p(T)**

where α is the thermal diffusivity from the flash measurement, ρ is the specimen density (measured by Archimedes' method per ASTM D792 or geometric measurement), and c_p is the specific heat capacity measured independently by DSC per ASTM E1269 or by comparative measurement against a reference in the LFA itself (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000039). The NETZSCH reference material set includes Pyroceram 9606, POCO graphite, and Inconel 600, with certified thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity values up to 1000 °C. ## Summary of Key Numerical Parameters for Animation Reference

- **Sample mass for DSC:** 10–25 mg (Al alloys), ~20 mg typical (pqac-00000048)
- **Alumina crucible volume:** ~85 µL (STA 449 configuration) (pqac-00000039)
- **Crucible outer diameter:** ~6.8 mm (Pt-Rh for STA 449) (pqac-00000000); standalone Al₂O₃ crucibles approximately 5–8 mm (pqac-00000025)
- **Argon purge flow:** 35–80 mL/min (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000040)
- **Heating/cooling rates:** 3–20 K/min typical (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000047)
- **Peak temperature, Al alloys:** 720–850 °C (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000020)
- **Peak temperature, Cu alloys (NAB):** 1100 °C (pqac-00000041)
- **LFA specimen:** 10 × 10 × 2 mm or ø 12.7 × 1–3 mm (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005)
- **LFA shots per temperature:** 3 (pqac-00000039)
- **LFA purge flow:** 50–80 mL/min (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000040)
- **Microbalance readability:** <10 µg (pqac-00000015)
- **Calibration standard masses:** 10–40 mg (pqac-00000014)
- **Calibration metals:** In (156.6 °C), Zn (419.5 °C), Al (660.3 °C), Ag (961.8 °C), Au (1064.2 °C) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018)

Where platinum crucibles must be used (e.g., for cp measurements per ASTM E1269), an alumina liner must be inserted to prevent contact between the melt and platinum (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000029).

### 2.4 Furnace Loading, Evacuation, and Backfilling

The operator positions the loaded sample crucible and an identical empty reference crucible symmetrically on the sensor contact faces (pqac-00000025). The furnace is lowered (or the hoist raises it) and sealed. For the NETZSCH DSC 404 F1, the roughing pump and turbomolecular pump are engaged to evacuate the measurement chamber (pqac-00000023). The chamber is then backfilled with high-purity argon (≥99.999 %). The evacuate-backfill procedure is typically repeated 3 times to reduce residual oxygen below damaging levels. A continuous purge of argon is then established; published flow rates are 35 mL/min (pqac-00000048), 50 mL/min (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028), or 60 mL/min (pqac-00000039).

### 2.5 Temperature Program

A typical temperature program for Al-alloy solidification (e.g., AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) involves: heating from room temperature at 3–20 K/min to 720–850 °C (approximately 50–100 °C above the alloy liquidus), holding isothermally for 5 min to achieve complete melting and thermal equilibration, then cooling at a controlled rate (3–20 K/min, or as low as 0.6 K/min for near-equilibrium solidification studies) back to room temperature (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Commonly, two or three consecutive heating-cooling cycles are performed; the second heating is considered more representative because the first cooling homogenises the microstructure (pqac-00000048). For Cu-alloy (NAB) work, the temperature program extends to 1100 °C, with heating and cooling at 5 K/min and a 5-minute isothermal hold at peak temperature (pqac-00000041).

### 2.6 Post-Run Checks

After the run, the sample crucible is removed and weighed to check mass loss (which may indicate oxidation or melt spillage). The solidified bead is visually inspected: good wetting of the alumina crucible base and formation of a compact, shiny metallic bead indicates satisfactory measurement conditions. Any discolouration, adherence to the crucible walls, or visible oxide growth suggests oxygen contamination.

## 3. Calibration with Pure-Metal Standards

### 3.1 Reference Materials and Procedures

Temperature and enthalpy calibration follows ASTM E967 (temperature) and E968 (enthalpy). The calibration uses high-purity metals with certified melting points and enthalpies of fusion:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Nominal melting temperatures and enthalpies of fusion: In (156.6 °C, 28.71 ± 0.08 J/g), Zn (419.5 °C, 108.6 ± 0.5 J/g), Al (660.3 °C, 401.3 ± 1.6 J/g), Ag (961.8 °C), and Au (1064.2 °C), each with an expanded uncertainty (k = 2) of 0.2 °C on the melting temperature (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

### 3.2 Sample Masses and Procedure

Calibration specimens are prepared with low masses, mostly 10–40 mg, to obtain sharper melting peaks and reduce uncertainty in the onset temperature determination (pqac-00000014). Conventional calibration is typically performed at 10 mg sample mass and 10 °C/min heating rate (pqac-00000012). Calibration is performed in the same crucible type, atmosphere, and configuration as the actual measurements; heating rates of 2–20 K/min are used (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000047).

### 3.3 Onset and Enthalpy Determination

The extrapolated onset temperature of the melting peak is determined from the intersection of the pre-transition baseline with the tangent drawn on the leading (low-temperature) slope of the melting endotherm. This onset temperature is compared with the nominal melting point; the resulting temperature offset is interpolated across the full calibration range using a polynomial or piecewise-linear fit (pqac-00000015). For enthalpy calibration, the melting endotherm is integrated between baseline-corrected limits, and the calculated heat of fusion is compared with the certified value (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018). A minimum of three calibration substances spanning the measurement temperature range is recommended, though more are preferred (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000017).

### 3.4 Acceptable Deviations

ASTM E968 reports a heat-calibration repeatability of 0.94 % at the indium melting point and 1.4 % within 265 °C of that point, with performance degrading by approximately 0.7 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Reproducibility is 2.7 % within 265 °C, decreasing by 2.0 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Extrapolation of a single-point indium calibration to high temperatures can produce unacceptable reproducibility—up to 25 % (pqac-00000016). ASTM D3418 acceptance criteria specify ±4.2 °C for onset melting-temperature reproducibility and ±7.3 % for enthalpy (pqac-00000012).

### 3.5 Thermal-Lag Correction

The thermal-lag contribution can be estimated from the temperature shift equation ΔT = T_max − T₀ = 2 ΔH_m R β + τ_lag β, where τ_lag represents the thermal delay, β is the heating rate, and R is the total thermal resistance (pqac-00000012). The trailing edge (high-temperature side) of a pure-metal melting peak depends on the total thermal resistance and the sample heat capacity, while the leading slope reflects the inverse total thermal resistance (pqac-00000019). By examining the return of the signal to baseline after the melting peak at several heating rates, the instrument time constant τ can be extracted. This time constant is then used to deconvolute measured DSC signals and correct for smearing effects, particularly important at higher heating rates or for samples with high thermal resistance (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000019). Calibration should be performed and verified approximately every two months (pqac-00000018).

## 4. Laser Flash Thermal Diffusivity (ASTM E1461)

### 4.1 Instruments

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**NETZSCH LFA 457 MicroFlash.** A laser-flash system operating from 20 to 1100 °C. It employs a pulsed laser as the flash source and contains a three-sample carousel inside a quartz tube with SiC heating elements. The system has a rotary pump for evacuating and backfilling gases. During normal operation, tests are performed under high-purity purge gas (Ar, N₂, or He) at 80 mL/min flow rate (pqac-00000040).

**NETZSCH LFA 467 HyperFlash/HT.** A xenon-flash-lamp-based system capable of testing from room temperature to 1200 °C. It has four small individual furnaces on a motor-controlled base and a turbomolecular pump achieving vacuum levels below 10⁻⁴ torr. It can test oxygen-sensitive materials (tungsten, graphite) using ultra-high-purity argon with gettering (pqac-00000040). The xenon flash lamp provides software-controlled pulse energy up to 10 J per pulse (pqac-00000035).

Both systems follow ASTM E1461 for design and data analysis (pqac-00000040).

### 4.2 Specimen Geometry and Preparation

Specimens are typically 10 × 10 × 2 mm squares (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000039) or round disks of 12.7 mm or 6.35 mm diameter (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000034). Standard specimens are 10 mm diameter × 1–2 mm thick; miniature specimens of 3 mm diameter × 0.5 mm thick have been validated (pqac-00000030). Recommended thickness depends on diffusivity: 1–1.5 mm for low, 1.5–2 mm for medium, and 2–3 mm for high diffusivity materials (pqac-00000005). Specimens must have flat, parallel surfaces. For LFA of printed Al-alloy coupons, specimens are machined or wire-EDM cut to the required geometry and thickness.

**Graphite coating.** Both faces of each specimen are coated with a thin, uniform layer of graphite spray (e.g., Graphit-33 carbon spray) to increase absorptivity of the flash energy and improve emissivity for the infrared detector (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000030). Solvent-clean the specimen first, then apply several thin spray passes, allowing 2–5 minutes of drying between coats; three thin coats per face is a documented practice (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000005). For semi-transparent materials such as Pyroceram 9606, a metallic layer (Pt or Au) may be needed on each side to prevent light penetration (pqac-00000040).

### 4.3 Sample Holder and IR Detector

Specimens are placed in holder plates within the sample tray and covered by a mask with an opening centred over each specimen (pqac-00000031). The LFA 447 NanoFlash uses a liquid-nitrogen-cooled InSb (indium antimonide) infrared detector sensitive to 1–5 µm wavelengths (pqac-00000034). Commercial laser-flash systems generally employ Nd:YAG pulsed lasers or xenon flash lamps with millisecond or microsecond pulse durations (pqac-00000009).

### 4.4 Measurement Sequence

A typical measurement sequence involves:
1. Stabilise the specimen at the programmed temperature isothermally.
2. Fire the flash pulse; record the time-dependent temperature rise on the rear face with the IR detector.
3. Wait for the specimen to return to the furnace equilibrium temperature.
4. Repeat: three shots are taken at each temperature to ensure reproducibility (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000039).
5. Step to the next programmed temperature (e.g., at 20 °C intervals from 25 to 500 °C) and repeat (pqac-00000029).

The measurement duration is set to approximately ten times the half-rise time (t₁/₂), and the maximum temperature rise is adjusted to approximately two-fifths of the horizontal measurement window (pqac-00000008). Data are fitted using the Cowan model with pulse correction, the Cape-Lehman model, or the Parker model, depending on heat-loss conditions and pulse duration relative to t₁/₂ (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000039). Reported measurement accuracy is ±3 % for thermal diffusivity and ±5 % for specific heat, with repeatability of ±2 % and ±3 %, respectively (pqac-00000011).

### 4.5 Thermal Conductivity Computation

Thermal conductivity is computed from the relationship:

**k(T) = α(T) × ρ(T) × c_p(T)**

where α is the thermal diffusivity from the flash measurement, ρ is the specimen density (measured by Archimedes' method per ASTM D792 or geometric measurement), and c_p is the specific heat capacity measured independently by DSC per ASTM E1269 or by comparative measurement against a reference in the LFA itself (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000039). The reference material for c_p via LFA is typically Pyroceram 9606, POCO graphite, or a copper standard of known properties, with matched dimensions, coating, and test conditions (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

### 4.6 Reference Materials for LFA System Validation

The NETZSCH reference material set includes Pyroceram 9606, POCO graphite, and Inconel 600, with certified thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity values up to 1000 °C. For moderate-to-high conductivity materials (such as Al alloys), Inconel 600 is the preferred reference material due to its consistency, durability, and simple sample preparation—it is opaque and requires only a graphite spray coating (pqac-00000040).

## Summary of Key Numerical Parameters for Animation Reference

- **Sample mass for DSC:** 10–25 mg (Al alloys), ~20 mg typical (pqac-00000048)
- **Alumina crucible volume:** ~85 µL (STA 449 configuration) (pqac-00000039)
- **Crucible outer diameter:** ~6.8 mm (Pt-Rh for STA 449) (pqac-00000000); standalone Al₂O₃ crucibles approximately 5–8 mm (pqac-00000025)
- **Argon purge flow:** 35–80 mL/min (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000040)
- **Heating/cooling rates:** 3–20 K/min typical (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000047)
- **Peak temperature, Al alloys:** 720–850 °C (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000020)
- **Peak temperature, Cu alloys (NAB):** 1100 °C (pqac-00000041)
- **LFA specimen:** 10 × 10 × 2 mm or ø 12.7 × 1–3 mm (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005)
- **LFA shots per temperature:** 3 (pqac-00000039)
- **LFA purge flow:** 50–80 mL/min (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000040)
- **Microbalance readability:** <10 µg (pqac-00000015)
- **Calibration standard masses:** 10–40 mg (pqac-00000014)
- **Calibration metals:** In (156.6 °C), Zn (419.5 °C), Al (660.3 °C), Ag (961.8 °C), Au (1064.2 °C) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018)
