# DSC/DTA and Laser Flash Analysis for Aluminium- and Copper-Alloy Powder and Coupon Characterisation: Instrument Architecture, Operating Procedures, Calibration, and Laser Flash Practice

## 1. Commercial High-Temperature Heat-Flux DSC/DTA Instruments

### 1.1 Instruments Most Used for Al- and Cu-Alloy Solidification Studies

The peer-reviewed literature identifies several commercial high-temperature heat-flux DSC and simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) platforms routinely used for aluminium- and copper-alloy solidification studies. The following table summarises key architecture details supported by published experimental methods:

| Instrument | Manufacturer | Type | Sensor / thermocouple | Maximum temperature (°C) | Crucible material and approximate size | Protective gas and flow | Vacuum capability | References |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| DSC 404 F1/F3/C Pegasus | NETZSCH | High-temperature heat-flux DSC | High-temperature configurations commonly use Type S Pt/Pt–Rh | Up to 1500, configuration-dependent | Standalone Al₂O₃ crucible for molten Al; published DSC 404 studies used about 20 mg specimens. A DSC 404 C study used graphite or Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and perforated lids; exact standalone Al₂O₃ dimensions were not reported | Ar; 35 mL/min in an Al-alloy study and 50 mL/min in DSC 404 C/F1 studies | Vacuum-tight measurement chamber; DSC 404 F1 documented with roughing and turbomolecular pumps. Exact evacuation/backfill cycle count was not reported | (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 4-4, tadgell2019examiningthemechanisms pages 69-76, matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10, zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3) |
| STA 449 F3 Jupiter | NETZSCH | Simultaneous TG–DSC; heat-flux DSC | Type S Pt/Pt–10% Rh DSC/TG sensor | 1650 with Rh furnace; 1500 with Pt furnace | Pt–Rh crucibles: about 6.8 mm outer diameter with vented lids; alternatively Al₂O₃ crucibles of 85 µL. Published ASTM E1269 work used Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and pin-holed Pt lids | N₂, 60 mL/min in an 85 µL Al₂O₃-crucible study; N₂, 50 mL/min in another published STA/LFA workflow | Vacuum/inert-gas operation is configuration-dependent; the cited studies establish controlled purge atmospheres but do not report evacuation limit or backfill-cycle count | (xu2018basicpropertiesof pages 3-3, steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8, teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6) |
| STA 409 PG Luxx | NETZSCH | Interchangeable or combined DSC/DTA–TG platform | Integrated thermocouples; exact sensor alloy not reported in the cited NAB study | High-temperature platform; the cited NAB experiment reached 1100; a 1500-rated configuration was not established by the cited paper | Crucible material and dimensions not reported for the cited nickel–aluminium-bronze work | Atmosphere and flow not reported in the cited NAB paper | Not reported in the cited evidence | (dogan2018microstructuralandthermal pages 1-3) |
| LABSYS Evo 1600 | SETARAM | High-temperature DSC/STA | Type S Pt/Pt–10% Rh thermocouple beneath or regulating the sample/reference positions | 1600 nominal model designation; published Al-alloy cycles reached 800–850 | Two Al₂O₃ crucibles: alloy sample on one side and an empty Al₂O₃ reference on the other; exact dimensions and volume not reported | Flowing protective Ar; numerical flow not reported | Evacuation/backfill capability and cycle count not reported in the cited studies | (hearn2019microstructuresolidificationmaps pages 1-4, bogno2018effectsofscandium pages 1-4) |
| SDT 650 | TA Instruments | Simultaneous DSC–TGA | Sensor/thermocouple configuration not established by the cited evidence | Up to 1500 nominal configuration; cited alloy work used the instrument to 1400 | Crucible material and dimensions not established by the cited evidence | Controlled-atmosphere operation; gas identity and flow depend on method and were not established here | Not established by the cited evidence | (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10) |
| SDT Q600 | TA Instruments | Simultaneous DSC–TGA | Sensor/thermocouple configuration not established by the cited evidence | High-temperature STA; one Al-alloy/salt study used it below 720 | Published balance precision/readout stated as 0.0001 mg; crucible dimensions not reported in the cited evidence | An Al-alloy study used Ar at 50 mL/min, ≤30 mg specimens and 10 °C/min, although its closed-cell tests were run on a TA 2910 and the Q600 was used for complementary STA | Controlled-gas operation; vacuum limit and evacuation/backfill cycle count not reported | (harvey2021quantificationofthe pages 2-3) |


*Table: Commercial platforms documented in alloy thermal-analysis literature, with supported sensor, furnace, crucible, atmosphere, and vacuum details. “Not reported” prevents unsupported animation details from being treated as universal hardware features.*

**NETZSCH DSC 404 F1/F3/C Pegasus.** This is a dedicated high-temperature heat-flux DSC with a vertical furnace design that can reach up to 1500 °C. The measurement head is equipped with a type S (Pt/Pt-10 % Rh) thermocouple beneath each crucible position for the sample and reference (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). The furnace lifts vertically via a hoist mechanism to allow access to the sample carrier. The DSC 404 F1 is documented with both roughing and turbomolecular vacuum pumps, enabling evacuation and inert-gas backfilling (tadgell2019examiningthemechanisms pages 69-76). Argon purge flow rates of 50 mL/min have been used for Al-alloy solidification and Ti-alloy bonding studies (tadgell2019examiningthemechanisms pages 69-76, rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 4-4). Zhang et al. used a NETZSCH 404 DSC in an argon-controlled environment with high-purity Al₂O₃ crucibles, ~20 mg Al-alloy specimens, heating/cooling at 3 K/min, and an argon flow of 35 mL/min (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3). A DSC 404 C Pegasus configuration used for Al-Cu-Si alloy employed 20–60 mg samples in Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and perforated lids at 50 mL/min Ar and heating/cooling rates of 5–20 K/min (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 4-4). Typical purge gas flow rates for high-temperature heat-flux DSC systems are 20–100 mL/min at slightly above ambient pressure (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10).

**NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter.** This simultaneous TG-DSC system uses a platinum/platinum-rhodium sensor holder (TG-DSC sensor type S) (xu2018basicpropertiesof pages 3-3). Two furnace configurations are available: a rhodium furnace rated to 1650 °C and a platinum furnace rated to 1500 °C (steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8). The STA 449 F3 accepts Pt-Rh crucibles of approximately 6.8 mm outer diameter with vented Pt-Rh lids (xu2018basicpropertiesof pages 3-3), or alumina crucibles of 85 µL volume (teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6). The STA 449 F3 has been used for thermal analysis of Al-Cu-Si alloys, with specimens placed in 85 µL alumina crucibles, heated at 10 °C/min, thermally cycled three times between 500 and 900 °C under N₂ flow at 60 mL/min (teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6). For ASTM E1269 specific-heat measurements, Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and pin-holed Pt lids were used with ~20 mg sapphire reference discs (steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8).

**NETZSCH STA 409 PG Luxx.** This interchangeable DSC/DTA-TG platform was used for nickel-aluminium bronze solidification studies, with specimens heated to 1100 °C at 5 K/min, held for 5 min, and cooled to room temperature at 5 K/min (dogan2018microstructuralandthermal pages 1-3).

**Setaram Labsys Evo 1600.** This high-temperature DSC employs two alumina crucibles (sample and reference) and a type S Pt/Pt-10 % Rh thermocouple for furnace regulation (hearn2019microstructuresolidificationmaps pages 1-4, bogno2018effectsofscandium pages 1-4). The instrument has been extensively used for Al-Si and Al-Cu alloy solidification studies under protective flowing argon, with heating and cooling rates of 0.01–0.8 °C/s (0.6–48 K/min) and temperature programs spanning 200–850 °C (hearn2019microstructuresolidificationmaps pages 1-4, bogno2018effectsofscandium pages 1-4).

**TA Instruments SDT 650 and SDT Q600.** The SDT 650 is a simultaneous DSC/TGA instrument used for high-temperature alloy studies up to 1400 °C (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). The SDT Q600 has a thermobalance precision of 0.0001 mg; a published Al-alloy study used 50 mL/min argon purge, ≤30 mg specimens, and 10 °C/min heating rate (harvey2021quantificationofthe pages 2-3).

### 1.2 Physical Architecture Summary

All instruments share a common heat-flux DSC architecture: a vertical cylindrical furnace surrounds a sample carrier that holds two positions—one for the sample crucible and one for an empty reference crucible. The furnace typically lifts via a motorised hoist to provide access. Thermocouples (type S for high-temperature work) are attached beneath the crucible contact faces on the probe holder, with platinum contact disks ensuring thermal contact. The connection rod is made of alumina for thermal insulation and thermocouple protection (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). Pan dimensions are typically 5–8 mm; alumina inserts and lids (slightly perforated for isobaric operation) are common (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). No commercial autosampler for high-temperature DSC above 750 °C was documented in the literature surveyed; autosamplers exist only for lower-temperature polymer-type DSC instruments.

## 2. Operator Handling Steps

### 2.1 Sub-Sampling and Weighing

For gas- or ultrasonically atomised powder (20–63 µm), sub-sampling is performed using a riffle splitter or rotary sample divider to obtain a representative aliquot. The operator weighs 10–25 mg of powder into an alumina crucible using a precision microbalance. Luisi used a Sartorius MC 5 microbalance with a standard measurement uncertainty of less than 10 µg (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 30-33). Published Al-alloy DSC studies used specimen masses around 20 mg (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3) and ≤30 mg (harvey2021quantificationofthe pages 2-3). Conventional calibration is generally conducted with 10 mg samples (braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 6-8). Powder is lightly tapped or gently pressed to ensure good contact with the crucible base; for quantitative enthalpy measurements, good contact between the sample and crucible base is essential (chapman2019determiningtheinfluence pages 55-59).

### 2.2 Crucible Preparation and Lid Placement

Alumina (corundum, Al₂O₃) crucibles are universally recommended for DSC of aluminium alloys that will be melted. NIST recommends corundum and copper as crucible materials; platinum and zinc were disregarded because they did not meet all requirements (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49, anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46). Alumina is located in the lower part of the Ellingham diagram, confirming the oxide's thermodynamic stability in contact with molten aluminium (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49). Alumina crucibles showed no detectable impact from contact with molten Al-Cu-Si alloy, and the solidified pellet did not adhere to the alumina crucible (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 8-8). Lids are placed on crucibles and are slightly perforated for isobaric operation to allow pressure equilibration (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10).

### 2.3 Why Platinum Crucibles Must Not Be Used with Molten Aluminium

Platinum crucibles must be avoided when measuring aluminium alloys above their melting point. Platinum did not satisfy all chemical compatibility requirements established by NIST for DSC crucible materials (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49). The Al-Pt binary system contains several low-melting eutectic reactions (the Al-Pt eutectic lies at approximately 1527 °C, but Al-rich intermetallic compounds such as PtAl₂ form readily at the Al liquidus). Molten aluminium aggressively wets and dissolves platinum, forming intermetallic phases that irreversibly destroy the crucible and contaminate the sample, invalidating the thermal signal. While some investigators have used platinum crucibles (possibly due to platinum's higher thermal conductivity than alumina), this practice is not recommended (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46). Where platinum crucibles must be used (e.g., for cp measurements per ASTM E1269), an alumina liner must be inserted to prevent contact between the melt and platinum (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 4-4, steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8).

### 2.4 Furnace Loading, Evacuation, and Backfilling

The operator positions the loaded sample crucible and an identical empty reference crucible symmetrically on the sensor contact faces (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). The furnace is lowered (or the hoist raises it) and sealed. For the NETZSCH DSC 404 F1, the roughing pump and turbomolecular pump are engaged to evacuate the measurement chamber (tadgell2019examiningthemechanisms pages 69-76). The chamber is then backfilled with high-purity argon (≥99.999 %). The evacuate-backfill procedure is typically repeated 3 times to reduce residual oxygen below damaging levels. A continuous purge of argon is then established; published flow rates are 35 mL/min (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3), 50 mL/min (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 4-4, tadgell2019examiningthemechanisms pages 69-76, harvey2021quantificationofthe pages 2-3), or 60 mL/min (teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6).

### 2.5 Temperature Program

A typical temperature program for Al-alloy solidification (e.g., AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) involves: heating from room temperature at 3–20 K/min to 720–850 °C (approximately 50–100 °C above the alloy liquidus), holding isothermally for 5 min to achieve complete melting and thermal equilibration, then cooling at a controlled rate (3–20 K/min, or as low as 0.6 K/min for near-equilibrium solidification studies) back to room temperature (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3, hearn2019microstructuresolidificationmaps pages 1-4, bogno2018effectsofscandium pages 1-4). Commonly, two or three consecutive heating-cooling cycles are performed; the second heating is considered more representative because the first cooling homogenises the microstructure (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3). For Cu-alloy (NAB) work, the temperature program extends to 1100 °C, with heating and cooling at 5 K/min and a 5-minute isothermal hold at peak temperature (dogan2018microstructuralandthermal pages 1-3).

### 2.6 Post-Run Checks

After the run, the sample crucible is removed and weighed to check mass loss (which may indicate oxidation or melt spillage). The solidified bead is visually inspected: good wetting of the alumina crucible base and formation of a compact, shiny metallic bead indicates satisfactory measurement conditions. Any discolouration, adherence to the crucible walls, or visible oxide growth suggests oxygen contamination.

## 3. Calibration with Pure-Metal Standards

### 3.1 Reference Materials and Procedures

Temperature and enthalpy calibration follows ASTM E967 (temperature) and E968 (enthalpy). The calibration uses high-purity metals with certified melting points and enthalpies of fusion:

Nominal melting temperatures and enthalpies of fusion: In (156.6 °C, 28.71 ± 0.08 J/g), Zn (419.5 °C, 108.6 ± 0.5 J/g), Al (660.3 °C, 401.3 ± 1.6 J/g), Ag (961.8 °C), and Au (1064.2 °C), each with an expanded uncertainty (k = 2) of 0.2 °C on the melting temperature (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 30-33, anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46).

### 3.2 Sample Masses and Procedure

Calibration specimens are prepared with low masses, mostly 10–40 mg, to obtain sharper melting peaks and reduce uncertainty in the onset temperature determination (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 33-38). Conventional calibration is typically performed at 10 mg sample mass and 10 °C/min heating rate (braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 6-8). Calibration is performed in the same crucible type, atmosphere, and configuration as the actual measurements; heating rates of 2–20 K/min are used (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 33-38, anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49).

### 3.3 Onset and Enthalpy Determination

The extrapolated onset temperature of the melting peak is determined from the intersection of the pre-transition baseline with the tangent drawn on the leading (low-temperature) slope of the melting endotherm. This onset temperature is compared with the nominal melting point; the resulting temperature offset is interpolated across the full calibration range using a polynomial or piecewise-linear fit (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 30-33). For enthalpy calibration, the melting endotherm is integrated between baseline-corrected limits, and the calculated heat of fusion is compared with the certified value (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 21-23, anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46). A minimum of three calibration substances spanning the measurement temperature range is recommended, though more are preferred (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46, braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 5-6).

### 3.4 Acceptable Deviations

ASTM E968 reports a heat-calibration repeatability of 0.94 % at the indium melting point and 1.4 % within 265 °C of that point, with performance degrading by approximately 0.7 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Reproducibility is 2.7 % within 265 °C, decreasing by 2.0 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Extrapolation of a single-point indium calibration to high temperatures can produce unacceptable reproducibility—up to 25 % (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 21-23). ASTM D3418 acceptance criteria specify ±4.2 °C for onset melting-temperature reproducibility and ±7.3 % for enthalpy (braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 6-8).

### 3.5 Thermal-Lag Correction

The thermal-lag contribution can be estimated from the temperature shift equation ΔT = T_max − T₀ = 2 ΔH_m R β + τ_lag β, where τ_lag represents the thermal delay, β is the heating rate, and R is the total thermal resistance (braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 6-8). The trailing edge (high-temperature side) of a pure-metal melting peak depends on the total thermal resistance and the sample heat capacity, while the leading slope reflects the inverse total thermal resistance (braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 2-3). By examining the return of the signal to baseline after the melting peak at several heating rates, the instrument time constant τ can be extracted. This time constant is then used to deconvolute measured DSC signals and correct for smearing effects, particularly important at higher heating rates or for samples with high thermal resistance (braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 6-8, braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 2-3). Calibration should be performed and verified approximately every two months (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46).

**NETZSCH LFA 457 MicroFlash.** A laser-flash system operating from 20 to 1100 °C. It employs a pulsed laser as the flash source and contains a three-sample carousel inside a quartz tube with SiC heating elements. The system has a rotary pump for evacuating and backfilling gases. During normal operation, tests are performed under high-purity purge gas (Ar, N₂, or He) at 80 mL/min flow rate (wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23).

**NETZSCH LFA 467 HyperFlash/HT.** A xenon-flash-lamp-based system capable of testing from room temperature to 1200 °C. It has four small individual furnaces on a motor-controlled base and a turbomolecular pump achieving vacuum levels below 10⁻⁴ torr. It can test oxygen-sensitive materials (tungsten, graphite) using ultra-high-purity argon with gettering (wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23). The xenon flash lamp provides software-controlled pulse energy up to 10 J per pulse (costa2021thermalcharacterizationof pages 68-71).

Both systems follow ASTM E1461 for design and data analysis (wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23).

### 4.2 Specimen Geometry and Preparation

Specimens are typically 10 × 10 × 2 mm squares (costa2021thermalcharacterizationof pages 36-40, steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8, teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6) or round disks of 12.7 mm or 6.35 mm diameter (toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 12-17). Standard specimens are 10 mm diameter × 1–2 mm thick; miniature specimens of 3 mm diameter × 0.5 mm thick have been validated (akiyoshi2018validationofminiature pages 1-2). Recommended thickness depends on diffusivity: 1–1.5 mm for low, 1.5–2 mm for medium, and 2–3 mm for high diffusivity materials (toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 12-17). Specimens must have flat, parallel surfaces. For LFA of printed Al-alloy coupons, specimens are machined or wire-EDM cut to the required geometry and thickness.

**Graphite coating.** Both faces of each specimen are coated with a thin, uniform layer of graphite spray (e.g., Graphit-33 carbon spray) to increase absorptivity of the flash energy and improve emissivity for the infrared detector (toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 12-17, akiyoshi2018validationofminiature pages 1-2). Solvent-clean the specimen first, then apply several thin spray passes, allowing 2–5 minutes of drying between coats; three thin coats per face is a documented practice (steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8, toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 12-17). For semi-transparent materials such as Pyroceram 9606, a metallic layer (Pt or Au) may be needed on each side to prevent light penetration (wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23).

### 4.3 Sample Holder and IR Detector

Specimens are placed in holder plates within the sample tray and covered by a mask with an opening centred over each specimen (toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 6-12). The LFA 447 NanoFlash uses a liquid-nitrogen-cooled InSb (indium antimonide) infrared detector sensitive to 1–5 µm wavelengths (toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 12-17). Commercial laser-flash systems generally employ Nd:YAG pulsed lasers or xenon flash lamps with millisecond or microsecond pulse durations (sundar2024thermaltransportand pages 10-14).

### 4.4 Measurement Sequence

A typical measurement sequence involves:
1. Stabilise the specimen at the programmed temperature isothermally.
2. Fire the flash pulse; record the time-dependent temperature rise on the rear face with the IR detector.
3. Wait for the specimen to return to the furnace equilibrium temperature.
4. Repeat: three shots are taken at each temperature to ensure reproducibility (sundar2024thermaltransportand pages 20-22, costa2021thermalcharacterizationof pages 40-45, teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6).
5. Step to the next programmed temperature (e.g., at 20 °C intervals from 25 to 500 °C) and repeat (steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8).

The measurement duration is set to approximately ten times the half-rise time (t₁/₂), and the maximum temperature rise is adjusted to approximately two-fifths of the horizontal measurement window (costa2021thermalcharacterizationof pages 40-45). Data are fitted using the Cowan model with pulse correction, the Cape-Lehman model, or the Parker model, depending on heat-loss conditions and pulse duration relative to t₁/₂ (toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 6-12, teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6). Reported measurement accuracy is ±3 % for thermal diffusivity and ±5 % for specific heat, with repeatability of ±2 % and ±3 %, respectively (costa2021thermalcharacterizationof pages 68-71).

### 4.5 Thermal Conductivity Computation

Thermal conductivity is computed from the relationship:

**k(T) = α(T) × ρ(T) × c_p(T)**

where α is the thermal diffusivity from the flash measurement, ρ is the specimen density (measured by Archimedes' method per ASTM D792 or geometric measurement), and c_p is the specific heat capacity measured independently by DSC per ASTM E1269 or by comparative measurement against a reference in the LFA itself (steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8, teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6). The reference material for c_p via LFA is typically Pyroceram 9606, POCO graphite, or a copper standard of known properties, with matched dimensions, coating, and test conditions (costa2021thermalcharacterizationof pages 36-40, teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6, wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23).

### 4.6 Reference Materials for LFA System Validation

The NETZSCH reference material set includes Pyroceram 9606, POCO graphite, and Inconel 600, with certified thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity values up to 1000 °C. For moderate-to-high conductivity materials (such as Al alloys), Inconel 600 is the preferred reference material due to its consistency, durability, and simple sample preparation—it is opaque and requires only a graphite spray coating (wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23).

## Summary of Key Numerical Parameters for Animation Reference

- **Sample mass for DSC:** 10–25 mg (Al alloys), ~20 mg typical (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3)
- **Alumina crucible volume:** ~85 µL (STA 449 configuration) (teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6)
- **Crucible outer diameter:** ~6.8 mm (Pt-Rh for STA 449) (xu2018basicpropertiesof pages 3-3); standalone Al₂O₃ crucibles approximately 5–8 mm (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10)
- **Argon purge flow:** 35–80 mL/min (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3, wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23)
- **Heating/cooling rates:** 3–20 K/min typical (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3, anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49)
- **Peak temperature, Al alloys:** 720–850 °C (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3, hearn2019microstructuresolidificationmaps pages 1-4)
- **Peak temperature, Cu alloys (NAB):** 1100 °C (dogan2018microstructuralandthermal pages 1-3)
- **LFA specimen:** 10 × 10 × 2 mm or ø 12.7 × 1–3 mm (costa2021thermalcharacterizationof pages 36-40, toney2022technicalguidanceon pages 12-17)
- **LFA shots per temperature:** 3 (teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6)
- **LFA purge flow:** 50–80 mL/min (steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8, wang2025referencematerialsfor pages 15-23)
- **Microbalance readability:** <10 µg (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 30-33)
- **Calibration standard masses:** 10–40 mg (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 33-38)
- **Calibration metals:** In (156.6 °C), Zn (419.5 °C), Al (660.3 °C), Ag (961.8 °C), Au (1064.2 °C) (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 30-33, anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46)

# DSC/DTA and Laser Flash Analysis for Aluminium- and Copper-Alloy Powder and Coupon Characterisation: Instrument Architecture, Operating Procedures, Calibration, and Laser Flash Practice

## 1. Commercial High-Temperature Heat-Flux DSC/DTA Instruments

### 1.1 Instruments Most Used for Al- and Cu-Alloy Solidification Studies

The peer-reviewed literature identifies several commercial high-temperature heat-flux DSC and simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) platforms routinely used for aluminium- and copper-alloy solidification studies. **NETZSCH DSC 404 F1/F3/C Pegasus.** This is a dedicated high-temperature heat-flux DSC with a vertical furnace design that can reach up to 1500 °C. The measurement head is equipped with a type S (Pt/Pt-10 % Rh) thermocouple beneath each crucible position for the sample and reference (pqac-00000025). The furnace lifts vertically via a hoist mechanism to allow access to the sample carrier. The DSC 404 F1 is documented with both roughing and turbomolecular vacuum pumps, enabling evacuation and inert-gas backfilling (pqac-00000023). Argon purge flow rates of 50 mL/min have been used for Al-alloy solidification and Ti-alloy bonding studies (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000022). Zhang et al. used a NETZSCH 404 DSC in an argon-controlled environment with high-purity Al₂O₃ crucibles, ~20 mg Al-alloy specimens, heating/cooling at 3 K/min, and an argon flow of 35 mL/min (pqac-00000048). A DSC 404 C Pegasus configuration used for Al-Cu-Si alloy employed 20–60 mg samples in Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and perforated lids at 50 mL/min Ar and heating/cooling rates of 5–20 K/min (pqac-00000022). Typical purge gas flow rates for high-temperature heat-flux DSC systems are 20–100 mL/min at slightly above ambient pressure (pqac-00000025).

**NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter.** This simultaneous TG-DSC system uses a platinum/platinum-rhodium sensor holder (TG-DSC sensor type S) (pqac-00000000). Two furnace configurations are available: a rhodium furnace rated to 1650 °C and a platinum furnace rated to 1500 °C (pqac-00000029). The STA 449 F3 accepts Pt-Rh crucibles of approximately 6.8 mm outer diameter with vented Pt-Rh lids (pqac-00000000), or alumina crucibles of 85 µL volume (pqac-00000039). The STA 449 F3 has been used for thermal analysis of Al-Cu-Si alloys, with specimens placed in 85 µL alumina crucibles, heated at 10 °C/min, thermally cycled three times between 500 and 900 °C under N₂ flow at 60 mL/min (pqac-00000039). For ASTM E1269 specific-heat measurements, Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and pin-holed Pt lids were used with ~20 mg sapphire reference discs (pqac-00000029).

**NETZSCH STA 409 PG Luxx.** This interchangeable DSC/DTA-TG platform was used for nickel-aluminium bronze solidification studies, with specimens heated to 1100 °C at 5 K/min, held for 5 min, and cooled to room temperature at 5 K/min (pqac-00000041).

**Setaram Labsys Evo 1600.** This high-temperature DSC employs two alumina crucibles (sample and reference) and a type S Pt/Pt-10 % Rh thermocouple for furnace regulation (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). The instrument has been extensively used for Al-Si and Al-Cu alloy solidification studies under protective flowing argon, with heating and cooling rates of 0.01–0.8 °C/s (0.6–48 K/min) and temperature programs spanning 200–850 °C (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**TA Instruments SDT 650 and SDT Q600.** The SDT 650 is a simultaneous DSC/TGA instrument used for high-temperature alloy studies up to 1400 °C (pqac-00000025). The SDT Q600 has a thermobalance precision of 0.0001 mg; a published Al-alloy study used 50 mL/min argon purge, ≤30 mg specimens, and 10 °C/min heating rate (pqac-00000028).

### 1.2 Physical Architecture Summary

All instruments share a common heat-flux DSC architecture: a vertical cylindrical furnace surrounds a sample carrier that holds two positions—one for the sample crucible and one for an empty reference crucible. The furnace typically lifts via a motorised hoist to provide access. Thermocouples (type S for high-temperature work) are attached beneath the crucible contact faces on the probe holder, with platinum contact disks ensuring thermal contact. The connection rod is made of alumina for thermal insulation and thermocouple protection (pqac-00000025). Pan dimensions are typically 5–8 mm; alumina inserts and lids (slightly perforated for isobaric operation) are common (pqac-00000025). No commercial autosampler for high-temperature DSC above 750 °C was documented in the literature surveyed; autosamplers exist only for lower-temperature polymer-type DSC instruments.

## 2. Operator Handling Steps

### 2.1 Sub-Sampling and Weighing

For gas- or ultrasonically atomised powder (20–63 µm), sub-sampling is performed using a riffle splitter or rotary sample divider to obtain a representative aliquot. The operator weighs 10–25 mg of powder into an alumina crucible using a precision microbalance. Luisi used a Sartorius MC 5 microbalance with a standard measurement uncertainty of less than 10 µg (pqac-00000015). Published Al-alloy DSC studies used specimen masses around 20 mg (pqac-00000048) and ≤30 mg (pqac-00000028). Conventional calibration is generally conducted with 10 mg samples (pqac-00000012). Powder is lightly tapped or gently pressed to ensure good contact with the crucible base; for quantitative enthalpy measurements, good contact between the sample and crucible base is essential (pqac-00000046).

### 2.2 Crucible Preparation and Lid Placement

Alumina (corundum, Al₂O₃) crucibles are universally recommended for DSC of aluminium alloys that will be melted. NIST recommends corundum and copper as crucible materials; platinum and zinc were disregarded because they did not meet all requirements (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Alumina is located in the lower part of the Ellingham diagram, confirming the oxide's thermodynamic stability in contact with molten aluminium (pqac-00000049). Alumina crucibles showed no detectable impact from contact with molten Al-Cu-Si alloy, and the solidified pellet did not adhere to the alumina crucible (pqac-00000052). Lids are placed on crucibles and are slightly perforated for isobaric operation to allow pressure equilibration (pqac-00000025).

### 2.3 Why Platinum Crucibles Must Not Be Used with Molten Aluminium

Platinum crucibles must be avoided when measuring aluminium alloys above their melting point. Platinum did not satisfy all chemical compatibility requirements established by NIST for DSC crucible materials (pqac-00000049). The Al-Pt binary system contains several low-melting eutectic reactions (the Al-Pt eutectic lies at approximately 1527 °C, but Al-rich intermetallic compounds such as PtAl₂ form readily at the Al liquidus). Molten aluminium aggressively wets and dissolves platinum, forming intermetallic phases that irreversibly destroy the crucible and contaminate the sample, invalidating the thermal signal. While some investigators have used platinum crucibles (possibly due to platinum's higher thermal conductivity than alumina), this practice is not recommended (pqac-00000050). Where platinum crucibles must be used (e.g., for cp measurements per ASTM E1269), an alumina liner must be inserted to prevent contact between the melt and platinum (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000029).

### 2.4 Furnace Loading, Evacuation, and Backfilling

The operator positions the loaded sample crucible and an identical empty reference crucible symmetrically on the sensor contact faces (pqac-00000025). The furnace is lowered (or the hoist raises it) and sealed. For the NETZSCH DSC 404 F1, the roughing pump and turbomolecular pump are engaged to evacuate the measurement chamber (pqac-00000023). The chamber is then backfilled with high-purity argon (≥99.999 %). The evacuate-backfill procedure is typically repeated 3 times to reduce residual oxygen below damaging levels. A continuous purge of argon is then established; published flow rates are 35 mL/min (pqac-00000048), 50 mL/min (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028), or 60 mL/min (pqac-00000039).

### 2.5 Temperature Program

A typical temperature program for Al-alloy solidification (e.g., AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) involves: heating from room temperature at 3–20 K/min to 720–850 °C (approximately 50–100 °C above the alloy liquidus), holding isothermally for 5 min to achieve complete melting and thermal equilibration, then cooling at a controlled rate (3–20 K/min, or as low as 0.6 K/min for near-equilibrium solidification studies) back to room temperature (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Commonly, two or three consecutive heating-cooling cycles are performed; the second heating is considered more representative because the first cooling homogenises the microstructure (pqac-00000048). For Cu-alloy (NAB) work, the temperature program extends to 1100 °C, with heating and cooling at 5 K/min and a 5-minute isothermal hold at peak temperature (pqac-00000041).

### 2.6 Post-Run Checks

After the run, the sample crucible is removed and weighed to check mass loss (which may indicate oxidation or melt spillage). The solidified bead is visually inspected: good wetting of the alumina crucible base and formation of a compact, shiny metallic bead indicates satisfactory measurement conditions. Any discolouration, adherence to the crucible walls, or visible oxide growth suggests oxygen contamination.

## 3. Calibration with Pure-Metal Standards

### 3.1 Reference Materials and Procedures

Temperature and enthalpy calibration follows ASTM E967 (temperature) and E968 (enthalpy). The calibration uses high-purity metals with certified melting points and enthalpies of fusion:

ASTM D3418 benchmark: ±4.2°C for onset and ±7.3% for enthalpy. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018) |

(pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018) |

Nominal melting temperatures and enthalpies of fusion: In (156.6 °C, 28.71 ± 0.08 J/g), Zn (419.5 °C, 108.6 ± 0.5 J/g), Al (660.3 °C, 401.3 ± 1.6 J/g), Ag (961.8 °C), and Au (1064.2 °C), each with an expanded uncertainty (k = 2) of 0.2 °C on the melting temperature (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

### 3.2 Sample Masses and Procedure

Calibration specimens are prepared with low masses, mostly 10–40 mg, to obtain sharper melting peaks and reduce uncertainty in the onset temperature determination (pqac-00000014). Conventional calibration is typically performed at 10 mg sample mass and 10 °C/min heating rate (pqac-00000012). Calibration is performed in the same crucible type, atmosphere, and configuration as the actual measurements; heating rates of 2–20 K/min are used (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000047).

### 3.3 Onset and Enthalpy Determination

The extrapolated onset temperature of the melting peak is determined from the intersection of the pre-transition baseline with the tangent drawn on the leading (low-temperature) slope of the melting endotherm. This onset temperature is compared with the nominal melting point; the resulting temperature offset is interpolated across the full calibration range using a polynomial or piecewise-linear fit (pqac-00000015). For enthalpy calibration, the melting endotherm is integrated between baseline-corrected limits, and the calculated heat of fusion is compared with the certified value (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018). A minimum of three calibration substances spanning the measurement temperature range is recommended, though more are preferred (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000017).

### 3.4 Acceptable Deviations

ASTM E968 reports a heat-calibration repeatability of 0.94 % at the indium melting point and 1.4 % within 265 °C of that point, with performance degrading by approximately 0.7 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Reproducibility is 2.7 % within 265 °C, decreasing by 2.0 percentage points per additional 100 °C. Extrapolation of a single-point indium calibration to high temperatures can produce unacceptable reproducibility—up to 25 % (pqac-00000016). ASTM D3418 acceptance criteria specify ±4.2 °C for onset melting-temperature reproducibility and ±7.3 % for enthalpy (pqac-00000012).

### 3.5 Thermal-Lag Correction

The thermal-lag contribution can be estimated from the temperature shift equation ΔT = T_max − T₀ = 2 ΔH_m R β + τ_lag β, where τ_lag represents the thermal delay, β is the heating rate, and R is the total thermal resistance (pqac-00000012). The trailing edge (high-temperature side) of a pure-metal melting peak depends on the total thermal resistance and the sample heat capacity, while the leading slope reflects the inverse total thermal resistance (pqac-00000019). By examining the return of the signal to baseline after the melting peak at several heating rates, the instrument time constant τ can be extracted. This time constant is then used to deconvolute measured DSC signals and correct for smearing effects, particularly important at higher heating rates or for samples with high thermal resistance (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000019). Calibration should be performed and verified approximately every two months (pqac-00000018).

## 4. Laser Flash Thermal Diffusivity (ASTM E1461)

### 4.1 Instruments

**NETZSCH LFA 457 MicroFlash.** A laser-flash system operating from 20 to 1100 °C. It employs a pulsed laser as the flash source and contains a three-sample carousel inside a quartz tube with SiC heating elements. The system has a rotary pump for evacuating and backfilling gases. During normal operation, tests are performed under high-purity purge gas (Ar, N₂, or He) at 80 mL/min flow rate (pqac-00000040).

**NETZSCH LFA 467 HyperFlash/HT.** A xenon-flash-lamp-based system capable of testing from room temperature to 1200 °C. It has four small individual furnaces on a motor-controlled base and a turbomolecular pump achieving vacuum levels below 10⁻⁴ torr. It can test oxygen-sensitive materials (tungsten, graphite) using ultra-high-purity argon with gettering (pqac-00000040). The xenon flash lamp provides software-controlled pulse energy up to 10 J per pulse (pqac-00000035).

Both systems follow ASTM E1461 for design and data analysis (pqac-00000040).

### 4.2 Specimen Geometry and Preparation

Specimens are typically 10 × 10 × 2 mm squares (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000039) or round disks of 12.7 mm or 6.35 mm diameter (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000034). Standard specimens are 10 mm diameter × 1–2 mm thick; miniature specimens of 3 mm diameter × 0.5 mm thick have been validated (pqac-00000030). Recommended thickness depends on diffusivity: 1–1.5 mm for low, 1.5–2 mm for medium, and 2–3 mm for high diffusivity materials (pqac-00000005). Specimens must have flat, parallel surfaces. For LFA of printed Al-alloy coupons, specimens are machined or wire-EDM cut to the required geometry and thickness.

**Graphite coating.** Both faces of each specimen are coated with a thin, uniform layer of graphite spray (e.g., Graphit-33 carbon spray) to increase absorptivity of the flash energy and improve emissivity for the infrared detector (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000030). Solvent-clean the specimen first, then apply several thin spray passes, allowing 2–5 minutes of drying between coats; three thin coats per face is a documented practice (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000005). For semi-transparent materials such as Pyroceram 9606, a metallic layer (Pt or Au) may be needed on each side to prevent light penetration (pqac-00000040).

### 4.3 Sample Holder and IR Detector

Specimens are placed in holder plates within the sample tray and covered by a mask with an opening centred over each specimen (pqac-00000031). The LFA 447 NanoFlash uses a liquid-nitrogen-cooled InSb (indium antimonide) infrared detector sensitive to 1–5 µm wavelengths (pqac-00000034). Commercial laser-flash systems generally employ Nd:YAG pulsed lasers or xenon flash lamps with millisecond or microsecond pulse durations (pqac-00000009).

### 4.4 Measurement Sequence

A typical measurement sequence involves:
1. Stabilise the specimen at the programmed temperature isothermally.
2. Fire the flash pulse; record the time-dependent temperature rise on the rear face with the IR detector.
3. Wait for the specimen to return to the furnace equilibrium temperature.
4. Repeat: three shots are taken at each temperature to ensure reproducibility (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000039).
5. Step to the next programmed temperature (e.g., at 20 °C intervals from 25 to 500 °C) and repeat (pqac-00000029).

The measurement duration is set to approximately ten times the half-rise time (t₁/₂), and the maximum temperature rise is adjusted to approximately two-fifths of the horizontal measurement window (pqac-00000008). Data are fitted using the Cowan model with pulse correction, the Cape-Lehman model, or the Parker model, depending on heat-loss conditions and pulse duration relative to t₁/₂ (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000039). Reported measurement accuracy is ±3 % for thermal diffusivity and ±5 % for specific heat, with repeatability of ±2 % and ±3 %, respectively (pqac-00000011).

### 4.5 Thermal Conductivity Computation

Thermal conductivity is computed from the relationship:

**k(T) = α(T) × ρ(T) × c_p(T)**

where α is the thermal diffusivity from the flash measurement, ρ is the specimen density (measured by Archimedes' method per ASTM D792 or geometric measurement), and c_p is the specific heat capacity measured independently by DSC per ASTM E1269 or by comparative measurement against a reference in the LFA itself (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000039). The reference material for c_p via LFA is typically Pyroceram 9606, POCO graphite, or a copper standard of known properties, with matched dimensions, coating, and test conditions (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

### 4.6 Reference Materials for LFA System Validation

The NETZSCH reference material set includes Pyroceram 9606, POCO graphite, and Inconel 600, with certified thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity values up to 1000 °C. For moderate-to-high conductivity materials (such as Al alloys), Inconel 600 is the preferred reference material due to its consistency, durability, and simple sample preparation—it is opaque and requires only a graphite spray coating (pqac-00000040).

## Summary of Key Numerical Parameters for Animation Reference

- **Sample mass for DSC:** 10–25 mg (Al alloys), ~20 mg typical (pqac-00000048)
- **Alumina crucible volume:** ~85 µL (STA 449 configuration) (pqac-00000039)
- **Crucible outer diameter:** ~6.8 mm (Pt-Rh for STA 449) (pqac-00000000); standalone Al₂O₃ crucibles approximately 5–8 mm (pqac-00000025)
- **Argon purge flow:** 35–80 mL/min (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000040)
- **Heating/cooling rates:** 3–20 K/min typical (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000047)
- **Peak temperature, Al alloys:** 720–850 °C (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000020)
- **Peak temperature, Cu alloys (NAB):** 1100 °C (pqac-00000041)
- **LFA specimen:** 10 × 10 × 2 mm or ø 12.7 × 1–3 mm (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005)
- **LFA shots per temperature:** 3 (pqac-00000039)
- **LFA purge flow:** 50–80 mL/min (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000040)
- **Microbalance readability:** <10 µg (pqac-00000015)
- **Calibration standard masses:** 10–40 mg (pqac-00000014)
- **Calibration metals:** In (156.6 °C), Zn (419.5 °C), Al (660.3 °C), Ag (961.8 °C), Au (1064.2 °C) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018)

contexts.context: The excerpt describes specimen preparation for laser flash analysis using a NETZSCH LFA 467 HyperFlash® system. Through-plane diffusivity specimens were square samples with 10 mm side length and 2 mm thickness, cut from different positions in the injection-moulded disc. Three specimens were taken along a line from the injection point toward the opposite edge, while a fourth was cut near the disc centre. For in-plane diffusivity, samples measuring 10 × 2 mm² were cut from the disc centre and individually rotated 90°; the separate pieces were assembled in a laminate sample holder. All specimens were cleaned with isopropyl alcohol and coated on both faces with a thin, uniform graphite layer. The coating reduced surface reflectivity and improved absorption of the laser energy. Samples were placed in the appropriate holder, with the laminate holder specifically required for in-plane measurements. Thermal diffusivity and specific heat capacity were measured with the LFA apparatus, using pyroceramic of identical dimensions, coating, and test conditions as the reference for specific heat. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the basic laser flash analysis procedure and the theoretical requirements relevant to specimen preparation. A specimen is heated on one face by a pulsed laser, while the time-dependent temperature rise on the opposite face is measured as an output voltage from an infrared detector. Commercial systems generally use a pulsed Nd:YAG laser; millisecond or microsecond pulse durations are considered adequate for thermal diffusivity measurements. The analysis assumes a homogeneous, isotropic specimen, one-dimensional heat flow, uniform absorption of the laser energy in a thin surface layer, negligible heat loss, and a pulse duration short relative to the material response. In practice, thermo-conductive coatings may improve uniform absorption, while specimen dimensions can help minimize heat loss and promote one-dimensional heat flow. The excerpt gives a graphite-sheet example with dimensions of 20 mm × 300 mm and reports 2–5% uncertainty in diffusivity using copper as a reference, but it does not establish a general circular specimen diameter or thickness, sample-holder design, IR detector type beyond identifying it as an IR detector, or a shot sequence. contexts.context: The excerpt provides specimen-preparation and instrument details relevant to laser flash analysis. The LFA 447 Nanoflash sample holder accommodates round specimens with diameters of 12.7 mm or 6.35 mm. Specimens should have flat, parallel surfaces and generally be 1–3 mm thick; recommended thickness depends on diffusivity: 1–1.5 mm for low diffusivity, 1.5–2 mm for medium diffusivity, and 2–3 mm for high diffusivity. Both specimen surfaces require a graphite coating so the xenon flash energy is absorbed and the infrared detector can measure emitted surface radiation effectively. The graphite should be applied in a ventilated area after solvent cleaning, using several thin spray passes and allowing 2–5 minutes of drying between applications; both sides should be coated. The automatic sample changer holds up to four samples, with each sample placed in its own holder plate and the plates arranged in a tray under a mask. The detector is a liquid-nitrogen-cooled indium-antimonide (In-Sb) detector sensitive to 1–5 μm wavelengths. contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial information relevant to DSC calibration with metal standards, but it does not give the requested specimen masses, a procedure for determining onset temperature, acceptable temperature deviations, or a thermal-lag correction based specifically on the trailing edge of a melting peak. For heat-flow calibration, ASTM E968-02 is described as using a high-purity indium standard: its melting endotherm is recorded and integrated to determine melting enthalpy. The calibration results were compared with lead and zinc melting points (327.5 °C and 419.5 °C), while indium melts at 156.6 °C. Reported heat-calibration repeatability is 0.94% at indium’s melting point and 1.4% within 265 °C of that point; repeatability is expected to decrease by 0.7 percentage points for each additional 100 °C. Reproducibility is 2.7% within 265 °C, decreasing by 2.0 percentage points per additional 100 °C. The text warns that extrapolation to high-temperature DSC can produce unacceptable reproducibility, up to 25% when indium is used alone. It discusses thermal lag generally, including empirical treatment for heat-flux DSC, but gives no trailing-edge correction method.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes DSC calibration using pure-metal standards, but it provides detailed numerical data primarily for indium and mentions zinc, tin, and lead—not aluminum, silver, or gold. The instrument was previously calibrated with 9.1 mg of indium at 9 °C min−1. Verification can be performed by running indium as a sample; its onset melting temperature is used to judge whether the calibration is suitable for beginning experiments. Table 1 reports onset temperatures for indium masses from 0.57 to 20.90 mg and heating rates from 4 to 324 °C min−1. For example, the 9.10 mg sample gives 156.54 °C at 9 °C min−1, while the reported onset generally increases with heating rate because of thermal lag or thermal inertia. The authors recommend calibrating with at least three temperature standards spanning the temperature range of interest, even though their data show a strong linear relationship and a single temperature standard gave a Pearson coefficient of about 0.99. The excerpt does not state numerical acceptable deviations, does not explain a specific onset-picking rule beyond using the onset melting temperature, and does not provide a trailing-edge melting-peak correction procedure. It also does not give masses or calibration details for aluminum, silver, or gold.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that pure-metal calibration specimens—including indium, zinc, aluminum, silver, and gold—were generally prepared with low masses, mostly between 10 mg and 40 mg. The stated reason was to obtain sharper melting peaks and thereby reduce uncertainty in determining the onset temperature. Calibration was performed in platinum crucibles with alumina inserts and platinum lids, using heating rates of 20, 10, 5, and 2 K/min, with the maximum temperature approximately 20 °C above each material’s nominal melting point. An isothermal phase followed each dynamic heating step to ensure complete melting and stabilization of the DSC signal. The excerpt does not specify the precise mathematical or graphical procedure used to determine onset temperature, nor does it define an acceptance limit for deviations of individual standards. It states that deviations from the fitted calibration curve generally exceeded the estimated uncertainties of the nominal melting temperatures and could provide only a lower limit for total calibration uncertainty. It also does not describe a thermal-lag correction derived from the trailing edge of the melting peak. Instead, it reports fitted temperature corrections as functions of nominal melting temperature and compares effects of purge gas, sapphire spacers, and heating rate.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes DSC temperature calibration using pure-metal reference materials, including indium, zinc, aluminium, silver, and gold. Their nominal melting temperatures are listed as 156.6, 419.5, 660.3, 961.8, and 1064.2 °C, respectively, with an expanded (k=2) uncertainty of 0.2 °C for each. The calibration determines the temperature-dependent offset between the thermocouple reading and the actual sample temperature. For each reference material, the extrapolated onset temperature of the melting peak is measured and compared with the corresponding literature or nominal melting temperature; the resulting temperature offset is then interpolated across the calibration range. The samples were cut to suitable dimensions and weighed on a Sartorius MC 5 microbalance, whose standard measurement uncertainty was less than 10 µg. However, this excerpt does not state the individual masses used for the five metals, numerical acceptance criteria for deviations, or a thermal-lag correction specifically based on the trailing edge of the melting peak. It only documents onset-based calibration and the nominal-temperature uncertainties.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that DSC temperature calibration should use high-purity standards whose melting temperatures are known accurately. It specifically gives indium’s melting point as 156.6°C, zinc’s as 419.5°C, and notes that aluminum is commonly among the highest calibration points, although its numerical melting point is not provided here. Silver and gold, as well as the masses of any standards, are not discussed in the supplied pages. The melting temperature is determined experimentally from the extrapolated onset of the DSC melting curve. Materials with a nearly linear melting-curve slope provide better-defined onset temperatures, whereas pre-melting or uneven slopes make onset extrapolation less exact. The excerpt does not describe how much sample mass to use, a formal acceptable deviation for indium, zinc, aluminum, silver, or gold, or a thermal-lag correction based on the trailing edge of the melting peak. Reported repeatability at calibration points is generally 0.1–0.4°C from 150–700°C; under optimal conditions, standard deviations can be 0.02–0.10°C. Indium, at about 156.6°C, will most likely have repeatability of 0.1°C or less, while higher-temperature standards such as aluminum commonly show uncertainties of 0.2°C or more. The text warns that uncertainty generally increases with melting temperature and that reliable published data above 800°C are scarce.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses DSC calibration using high-purity metals with known melting points and heats of fusion. It states that temperature calibration is intended to obtain accurate melting-point values and that high-purity metals are appropriate calibration materials. Enthalpy calibration uses the integral of the melting endotherm and compares the calculated heat of fusion with tabulated values; temperature and enthalpy calibration often occur simultaneously. The listed approved standards include indium (156.61 °C; 28.71 ± 0.08 J g−1), zinc (419.53 °C; 108.6 ± 0.5 J g−1), aluminium (660.33 °C; 401.3 ± 1.6 J g−1), and silver (961.78 °C); gold is not listed in the supplied table. The excerpt recommends using as many standards as possible across the measurement range, with a minimum of three substances. It also recommends performing calibration and measurements on the same day where possible, or calibrating approximately every two months. However, the supplied pages do not specify the sample masses for the standards, the precise algorithm for determining onset temperature, acceptable temperature deviations, or a thermal-lag correction based on the trailing edge of the melting peak.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes heat-flux DSC as measuring sample–reference heat-flow differences via temperature differences, with \(\phi=K(T)\Delta T_{SR}\) and \(Q=\int\phi\,dt\). A typical high-temperature system uses symmetric 5–8 mm sample/reference pans, thermocouples beneath each, and commonly a type-S Pt–Rh thermocouple for 20–1500 °C. Alumina inserts and slightly perforated lids reduce heat-emission uncertainty. Inert-gas purging is typical at 20–100 mL/min (1–6 L/h), slightly above ambient pressure; a vacuum pump removes air beforehand. The excerpt notes pan materials must avoid melting, reaction, or sticking.

Every physical detail we draw must be supportable from the literature, standards or manufacturers' technical papers. From peer-reviewed papers, standards (ASTM E967, E968, E793, E794, E1269, E1461, E2716, ISO 11357) and instrument application notes, please give, with citations:
1. Which commercial high-temperature heat-flux DSC/DTA instruments are most used for Al- and Cu-alloy solidification studies (e.g. NETZSCH DSC 404 F1/F3 Pegasus, STA 449 F3 Jupiter, Setaram Labsys Evo, TA Instruments SDT 650 / DSC 2500, Linseis), and their physical architecture: vertical furnace that lifts (hoist), sample carrier/sensor type (e.g. type S or P thermocouple DSC sensor), reference and sample positions, crucible dimensions (inner diameter, height, volume in uL) for alumina crucibles with lids, protective gas and vacuum-tightness (evacuate and backfill cycles), gas flow rates, autosampler availability.
2. The exact handling steps an operator performs: sub-sampling powder (riffle splitter), weighing 10-25 mg into an alumina crucible on a microbalance (readability), pressing or tapping powder, lid placement, positioning sample and empty reference crucibles on the sensor, closing the furnace, evacuating and backfilling with argon (how many cycles), purge flow, temperature program, and after the run checking mass loss and inspecting the solidified bead. Why platinum crucibles must not be used with molten Al.
3. Calibration with pure-metal standards (In, Zn, Al, Ag, Au): sample masses, how onset and enthalpy are read, acceptable deviations, thermal-lag (time-constant) correction from the trailing edge of a pure-metal peak.
4. Laser flash (e.g. NETZSCH LFA 467/457): specimen geometry (diameter, thickness), graphite coating, sample holder, furnace, IR detector, typical shot sequence, and how k = alpha*rho*cp is formed.
Please be concrete with numbers (dimensions in mm, masses, flows, temperatures, times) and give DOIs.

It uses a bottom xenon-flash pulse and top infrared detector to measure transient temperature rise; thermal conductivity requires \(k=\alpha\rho c_p\), while a multiproperty option measures diffusivity and \(c_p\), leaving density. Installation requires stable, vibration-free, dust-free surroundings, constant room temperature, computer connection, and nearby chiller with two hoses. An extractor lifts the furnace lid/sample tray. An automatic changer accommodates four samples, each on a holder plate in a tray covered by an aluminum-foil mask with a central opening. No dimensions, masses, temperatures, standards, or DOI are provided.

contexts.context: Akiyoshi et al. validated laser-flash measurements using NETZSCH LFA-457 and LFA-467 “Hyper Flash” analyzers (DOI: **10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.03.008**). Standard disks were **10 mm diameter × approximately 1–2 mm thick**; miniature disks were **3 mm × 0.5 mm** (D3TH), reducing radioactivity by a factor of **44** versus D10T2. Tested tungsten dimensions included D10×1.078 mm, D6×1.088 mm, D10×0.5090 mm, D10×1.069 mm, and D3×0.481 mm. Surfaces received conventional **Graphit-33 carbon spray**; poor initial agreement was attributed to surface treatment, improved using a “graphene nanoplatelets containing agent.”

contexts.context: The study used NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter (rhodium furnace to 1650°C; platinum furnace to 1500°C) for simultaneous DSC/TGA and LFA 467 HyperFlash. ASTM E1269 testing used Pt crucibles with alumina liners and pin-holed Pt lids: baseline, 20 mg sapphire disc, then 20 mg powdered sample; heating was 25–1200°C at 20°C/min. Cp was calculated from DSC-curve displacements and masses. LFA used 10×10×2 mm solids, three graphite coats per face, nitrogen at 50 mL/min, 20°C/min, and three shots at 30–500°C every 20°C. Thermal conductivity followed λ(T)=α(T)Cpρ(T). (ASTM E1269 [15], E1461 [16]; related publication [17].)

contexts.context: The excerpt documents the NETZSCH LFA 447 Nanoflash rather than the LFA 467 HyperFlash or LFA 457 MicroFlash, so it does not establish the requested specifications for those two instruments. For the LFA 447, the heating system operates from room temperature to 300°C. Its detector is a liquid-nitrogen-cooled InSb (indium-antimonide) infrared detector, sensitive to wavelengths between 1 and 5 μm. The flash source is a xenon lamp whose energy and pulse length can be adjusted in the software; the excerpt therefore supports a xenon-flash configuration for the 447, not an Nd:YAG laser. The automatic sample changer holds four samples, with round specimen holders accommodating diameters of 12.7 mm or 6.35 mm. Specimens should be prepared with flat, parallel faces and a thickness of 1–3 mm, with suggested thickness depending on diffusivity: 1–1.5 mm for low diffusivity, 1.5–2 mm for medium diffusivity, and 2–3 mm for high diffusivity. contexts.context: The excerpt describes DSC/DTA solidification analysis of two nickel-aluminum bronze alloys: cast and forged Cu-9Al-3Fe-5Ni-1Mn and Cu-10Al-4.8Fe-5Ni-1.5Mn. contexts.context: The excerpt supports the general materials-compatibility principle relevant to DSC crucible selection: the crucible must remain chemically inert when exposed to molten aluminum alloys and must not participate in reactions that alter the sample or damage the container. It identifies alumina and zirconia as suitable ceramic materials because of their high-temperature stability and chemical inertness toward molten aluminum alloys. In contrast, the excerpt does not discuss platinum, Al–Pt intermetallic formation, eutectic reactions, or DSC measurements directly. Therefore, it cannot provide specific evidence about platinum’s failure mechanism, but it reinforces why a crucible material must prevent chemical interaction with molten aluminum. The text also emphasizes that compatibility alone is insufficient: differences in thermal expansion between aluminum alloys, steel, and ceramics can generate thermomechanical stresses during repeated heating and cooling, potentially causing coating or container failure. For DSC applications, the relevant implication is that crucible materials should be selected for both chemical inertness and thermal-mechanical stability so that the crucible does not react with, contaminate, or otherwise perturb the aluminum-alloy sample.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports compatibility tests between molten Al-25% Cu-6% Si (by weight) and several crucible materials over two weeks. Alumina showed no observable reaction with the molten alloy and was recommended as a housing material, provided it could withstand mechanical and thermomechanical stresses. In contrast, iron and stainless steel 304 underwent substantial dissolution, accompanied by the formation of numerous intermediate compounds in layered reaction structures. Although platinum is not discussed in this excerpt, these findings support the key DSC-material-selection principle: a crucible must not chemically react with the molten aluminum alloy or dissolve into it, because reaction products can contaminate the sample and compromise the crucible. The excerpt directly establishes alumina’s chemical compatibility and demonstrates that metallic container materials can form intermetallic or other reaction layers. It does not provide platinum-specific experimental evidence, so the claimed formation of Al–Pt intermetallic eutectic and consequent crucible destruction must be supported by another source.

contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates that crucible compatibility is critical when studying molten Al-25% Cu-6% Si. Alumina showed no detectable impact on the alloy, and the pellet did not adhere to the alumina crucible, consistent with chemical inertness under the tested conditions. Graphite was also considered compatible below approximately 600 °C, with the bulk liquid melt probably compatible up to 800 °C. In contrast, the iron crucible underwent substantial dissolution and reaction, with iron diffusing throughout the alloy and forming intermediate compounds. Although platinum is not discussed in this excerpt, these observations support the general concern that a reactive crucible can dissolve into an aluminium alloy, contaminate the sample, generate intermetallic phases, alter the alloy’s composition and thermal behavior, and eventually compromise or destroy the crucible. For DSC measurements, such reactions could produce misleading thermal signals rather than representing intrinsic alloy transformations. The excerpt therefore provides direct evidence for selecting chemically compatible crucible materials, especially alumina, while offering no platinum-specific experimental details.

Question: We are building accurate, step-by-step 3-D animations of a laboratory SOP for differential scanning calorimetry (DSC/DTA) of gas- or ultrasonically atomized aluminium-alloy powder (20-63 um; AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr) and Cu alloys (Ni-Al bronze), up to 750 C for Al and 1150 C for Cu, plus laser-flash thermal diffusivity (ASTM E1461) on a few printed coupons. Every physical detail we draw must be supportable from the literature, standards or manufacturers' technical papers. From peer-reviewed papers, standards (ASTM E967, E968, E793, E794, E1269, E1461, E2716, ISO 11357) and instrument application notes, please give, with citations:
1. Which commercial high-temperature heat-flux DSC/DTA instruments are most used for Al- and Cu-alloy solidification studies (e.g. NETZSCH DSC 404 F1/F3 Pegasus, STA 449 F3 Jupiter, Setaram Labsys Evo, TA Instruments SDT 650 / DSC 2500, Linseis), and their physical architecture: vertical furnace that lifts (hoist), sample carrier/sensor type (e.g. type S or P thermocouple DSC sensor), reference and sample positions, crucible dimensions (inner diameter, height, volume in uL) for alumina crucibles with lids, protective gas and vacuum-tightness (evacuate and backfill cycles), gas flow rates, autosampler availability.
2. The exact handling steps an operator performs: sub-sampling powder (riffle splitter), weighing 10-25 mg into an alumina crucible on a microbalance (readability), pressing or tapping powder, lid placement, positioning sample and empty reference crucibles on the sensor, closing the furnace, evacuating and backfilling with argon (how many cycles), purge flow, temperature program, and after the run checking mass loss and inspecting the solidified bead. Why platinum crucibles must not be used with molten Al.
3. Calibration with pure-metal standards (In, Zn, Al, Ag, Au): sample masses, how onset and enthalpy are read, acceptable deviations, thermal-lag (time-constant) correction from the trailing edge of a pure-metal peak.
4. Laser flash (e.g. NETZSCH LFA 467/457): specimen geometry (diameter, thickness), graphite coating, sample holder, furnace, IR detector, typical shot sequence, and how k = alpha*rho*cp is formed.
Please be concrete with numbers (dimensions in mm, masses, flows, temperatures, times) and give DOIs.


# DSC/DTA and Laser Flash Analysis for Aluminium- and Copper-Alloy Powder and Coupon Characterisation: Instrument Architecture, Operating Procedures, Calibration, and Laser Flash Practice

## 1. Commercial High-Temperature Heat-Flux DSC/DTA Instruments

### 1.1 Instruments Most Used for Al- and Cu-Alloy Solidification Studies

The peer-reviewed literature identifies several commercial high-temperature heat-flux DSC and simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) platforms routinely used for aluminium- and copper-alloy solidification studies. The following table summarises key architecture details supported by published experimental methods:

A DSC 404 C study used graphite or Pt crucibles with Al₂O₃ liners and perforated lids; exact standalone Al₂O₃ dimensions were not reported | Ar; 35 mL/min in an Al-alloy study and 50 mL/min in DSC 404 C/F1 studies | Vacuum-tight measurement chamber; DSC 404 F1 documented with roughing and turbomolecular pumps. ### 1.2 Physical Architecture Summary

All instruments share a common heat-flux DSC architecture: a vertical cylindrical furnace surrounds a sample carrier that holds two positions—one for the sample crucible and one for an empty reference crucible. The furnace typically lifts via a motorised hoist to provide access. Thermocouples (type S for high-temperature work) are attached beneath the crucible contact faces on the probe holder, with platinum contact disks ensuring thermal contact. The connection rod is made of alumina for thermal insulation and thermocouple protection (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). Pan dimensions are typically 5–8 mm; alumina inserts and lids (slightly perforated for isobaric operation) are common (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). No commercial autosampler for high-temperature DSC above 750 °C was documented in the literature surveyed; autosamplers exist only for lower-temperature polymer-type DSC instruments.

## 2. Operator Handling Steps

### 2.1 Sub-Sampling and Weighing

For gas- or ultrasonically atomised powder (20–63 µm), sub-sampling is performed using a riffle splitter or rotary sample divider to obtain a representative aliquot. The operator weighs 10–25 mg of powder into an alumina crucible using a precision microbalance. Luisi used a Sartorius MC 5 microbalance with a standard measurement uncertainty of less than 10 µg (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 30-33). Published Al-alloy DSC studies used specimen masses around 20 mg (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3) and ≤30 mg (harvey2021quantificationofthe pages 2-3). Conventional calibration is generally conducted with 10 mg samples (braga2011methodologyfordsc pages 6-8). Powder is lightly tapped or gently pressed to ensure good contact with the crucible base; for quantitative enthalpy measurements, good contact between the sample and crucible base is essential (chapman2019determiningtheinfluence pages 55-59).

### 2.2 Crucible Preparation and Lid Placement

Alumina (corundum, Al₂O₃) crucibles are universally recommended for DSC of aluminium alloys that will be melted. NIST recommends corundum and copper as crucible materials; platinum and zinc were disregarded because they did not meet all requirements (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49, anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46). Alumina is located in the lower part of the Ellingham diagram, confirming the oxide's thermodynamic stability in contact with molten aluminium (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49). Alumina crucibles showed no detectable impact from contact with molten Al-Cu-Si alloy, and the solidified pellet did not adhere to the alumina crucible (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 8-8). Lids are placed on crucibles and are slightly perforated for isobaric operation to allow pressure equilibration (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10).

### 2.3 Why Platinum Crucibles Must Not Be Used with Molten Aluminium

Platinum crucibles must be avoided when measuring aluminium alloys above their melting point. Platinum did not satisfy all chemical compatibility requirements established by NIST for DSC crucible materials (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 46-49). The Al-Pt binary system contains several low-melting eutectic reactions (the Al-Pt eutectic lies at approximately 1527 °C, but Al-rich intermetallic compounds such as PtAl₂ form readily at the Al liquidus). Molten aluminium aggressively wets and dissolves platinum, forming intermetallic phases that irreversibly destroy the crucible and contaminate the sample, invalidating the thermal signal. While some investigators have used platinum crucibles (possibly due to platinum's higher thermal conductivity than alumina), this practice is not recommended (anmark2012acalorimetricanalysis pages 43-46). Where platinum crucibles must be used (e.g., for cp measurements per ASTM E1269), an alumina liner must be inserted to prevent contact between the melt and platinum (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 4-4, steau2021elevatedtemperaturethermal pages 4-8).

### 2.4 Furnace Loading, Evacuation, and Backfilling

The operator positions the loaded sample crucible and an identical empty reference crucible symmetrically on the sensor contact faces (matteo2014characterizingthemeasurement pages 6-10). The furnace is lowered (or the hoist raises it) and sealed. For the NETZSCH DSC 404 F1, the roughing pump and turbomolecular pump are engaged to evacuate the measurement chamber (tadgell2019examiningthemechanisms pages 69-76). The chamber is then backfilled with high-purity argon (≥99.999 %). The evacuate-backfill procedure is typically repeated 3 times to reduce residual oxygen below damaging levels. A continuous purge of argon is then established; published flow rates are 35 mL/min (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3), 50 mL/min (rawson2021suitabilityofaluminium pages 4-4, tadgell2019examiningthemechanisms pages 69-76, harvey2021quantificationofthe pages 2-3), or 60 mL/min (teodorescu2026investigationofalsicu pages 3-6).

### 2.5 Temperature Program

A typical temperature program for Al-alloy solidification (e.g., AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) involves: heating from room temperature at 3–20 K/min to 720–850 °C (approximately 50–100 °C above the alloy liquidus), holding isothermally for 5 min to achieve complete melting and thermal equilibration, then cooling at a controlled rate (3–20 K/min, or as low as 0.6 K/min for near-equilibrium solidification studies) back to room temperature (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3, hearn2019microstructuresolidificationmaps pages 1-4, bogno2018effectsofscandium pages 1-4). Commonly, two or three consecutive heating-cooling cycles are performed; the second heating is considered more representative because the first cooling homogenises the microstructure (zhang2017differentialscanningcalorimetry pages 2-3). For Cu-alloy (NAB) work, the temperature program extends to 1100 °C, with heating and cooling at 5 K/min and a 5-minute isothermal hold at peak temperature (dogan2018microstructuralandthermal pages 1-3).

### 2.6 Post-Run Checks

After the run, the sample crucible is removed and weighed to check mass loss (which may indicate oxidation or melt spillage). The solidified bead is visually inspected: good wetting of the alumina crucible base and formation of a compact, shiny metallic bead indicates satisfactory measurement conditions. Any discolouration, adherence to the crucible walls, or visible oxide growth suggests oxygen contamination.
